[from source] (SRE p.57)
Heavy use of white-box with modest but critical use of black-box; black-box is symptom-oriented and about active problems; for paging it forces discipline. [from source] (SRE p.57)
latency, traffic, errors, saturation. [from source] (SRE p.57-58)
Latency: separate the latency of successes and errors; a slow error is worse than a fast error. [from source] (SRE p.58)
Errors: explicit (HTTP 500), implicit (200 with wrong content) and by policy (above 1 s is an error). [from source] (SRE p.58)

Saturation: emphasize the most constrained resource; systems degrade before 100%; p99 in a short window is an early signal; saturation also involves predicting imminent saturation (e.g. "disk fills in 4 hours"), and you page when the signal is problematic or, in the case of saturation, "almost" problematic. [from source] (SRE p.58) Note 25 (p.62): zero-redundancy situations (N + 0) count as imminent, as do "almost full" parts of the service. [from source] (SRE p.62)
If you measure the four and page when one is problematic, the service is "decently covered". [from source] (SRE p.58)
Do not rely on averages: the p99 of a backend can become the median of the frontend; use latency buckets (histogram) with approximately exponential boundaries (factor ~3). [from source] (SRE p.58)

Resolution (p.59): granularity must follow the objective. Observing CPU over a one-minute window does not reveal long spikes that cause high tail latency (so CPU calls for a finer measurement than 1/min). On the other hand, for a web service with a 99.9% annual target (about 9 h of aggregate downtime per year), probing for status 200 more than once or twice a minute is probably too frequent; checking disk occupancy more than once every 1-2 minutes is also probably unnecessary. These are two distinct rules: "1-2 per minute" applies to probing for 200; "every 1-2 minutes" applies only to disk. For high resolution without high cost: internal sampling in the server (CPU every second, incrementing 5% buckets) and aggregation every minute by an external system. [from source] (SRE p.59)

Simple, predictable alert rules; remove rarely exercised collections and alerts (book example: a collection, aggregation or alert exercised less than once a quarter ("rarely exercised", "less than once a quarter") for some SRE teams is a removal candidate); signals collected but with no ready dashboard or alert are also removal candidates; separate monitoring from profiling, logging etc. [from source] (SRE p.59)

Granularity (p.59): for a service with a 99.9% target (about 9 hours of unavailability per year), probing for status 200 more than once or twice a minute is probably too frequent, and checking for a full disk more often than every 1-2 minutes also is; this 1-2 min threshold is on p.59 (printed 47). [from source] (SRE p.59)

Care with pages: "alert only on the urgent and actionable" (the questions and the philosophy of pages) is on p.59-60, whereas p.56 deals with why paging a human is expensive and with never alerting on "something odd". [from source] (SRE p.56, 59-60)
Five questions for a new alert (urgent/actionable/user-visible; will I ever be able to ignore it?; users affected?; can I act?; others paged?). [from source] (SRE p.59-60)
Philosophy of pages: urgency a few times a day, actionable, requires intelligence, concerns a new problem. [from source] (SRE p.60)

Cases: Bigtable (SLO by the mean generated too many alerts; remedy: improve, pull the SLO back to the p75, turn off email alerts) and Gmail (alerts per task; scripted stopgap vs definitive fix); red flag: a page with a robotic response. [from source] (SRE p.60-61)

Gmail/Workqueue (p.61): in the early days Gmail ran on Workqueue (a process manager adapted from search index batch) and alerts fired when each task was "de-scheduled"; with thousands of tasks, each a small fraction of users, this alert was unsustainable. The Gmail SRE built a tool that "poked" the scheduler without impacting users; the team debated automating the whole loop (detection → poke) until a better fix existed, but some feared delaying the real fix. The book says this tension reflects distrust of the team's self-discipline (the stopgap being forgotten or the fix being deprioritized), credible because patches create layers of technical debt; managers and technical leads must support and prioritize long-term fixes even when the initial pain of the pages passes. Red flag: pages with a routine, algorithmic response; refusing to automate them suggests a lack of confidence in paying down technical debt, a "bigger problem that deserves escalation". The book reviews paging statistics (incidents per shift) in quarterly reports with management. [from source] (SRE p.61)

An SRE team of 10-12 people typically has 1-2 dedicated to monitoring (a number that decreased with the centralization of infrastructure; every team has at least one "monitoring person"); teams avoid any situation that requires someone to "stare at a screen" to find problems. [from source] (SRE p.56) [DATED]

"Magic" systems and dependencies (p.56) [from source]: Google moved toward simpler and faster monitoring, with better tools for later analysis, and avoids "magic" systems that learn thresholds on their own or detect causality automatically (causality). Counterexample: rules about unexpected changes in the end-user request rate, kept as simple as possible, give very fast detection of a simple, specific and severe anomaly. Uses that tolerate more fragility (and complexity): capacity planning and traffic forecasting, and long-term observational experiments (months or years) with low sampling (hours or days), since lost samples do not hide the trend. Complex dependency hierarchies had limited success ("if the database is slow, alert the database; otherwise alert the slow site" is rare); dependent rules only appear in very stable parts, such as the system that drains traffic from a datacenter ("if the datacenter is drained, don't alert me about its latency"); few teams maintain complex hierarchies because the infrastructure is continuously refactored. (SRE p.56)

Borgmon collects metrics in a common format (/varz), keeps series in the "time-series arena" and evaluates rules centrally; Prometheus, Riemann, Heka and Bosun have similar principles. [from source] (SRE p.88-91, 98)
Counter (non-decreasing) vs gauge; prefer counters; rate() over a window. [from source] (SRE p.92-93)
Naming convention level:variable:operation (e.g. task:http_requests:rate10m). [from source] (SRE p.93)
Example alert: error ratio over 10 min > 1% AND errors > 1/s, for 2 min; flapping avoided by a minimum duration; labels with severity=page. [from source] (SRE p.95)
Alertmanager: inhibits, deduplicates, routes (pager, ticket, dashboard). [from source] (SRE p.95)
Prober (black-box) pointed at the frontend and the backend; configuration separates rules from targets; unit tests of rules. [from source] (SRE p.96-97)
It is not good to alert per individual machine at scale; aggregate and prune outliers. [from source] (SRE p.88)
The maintenance cost must scale sublinearly with the size of the service. [from source] (SRE p.97)

Borgmon keeps everything in an in-memory database with periodic checkpoints to disk; each point is (timestamp, value), in chronological lists (time-series) named by a set of name=value labels (var, job, service, zone are the minimum). In practice it is a fixed-size memory block, the "time-series arena", with a garbage collector that expires the oldest entries when the arena fills; the interval between the newest and the oldest entry is the horizon, that is, how much queryable data stays in RAM. [from source] (SRE p.90-91)

Sizing: datacenter and global Borgmon are sized for about 12 hours of data (to render consoles) and much less in the lowest-level collectors. A point costs about 24 bytes of memory, so "1 million unique series for 12 hours at 1-minute intervals fit in less than 17 GB of RAM". [from source] (SRE p.90-91)
The book does not say whether the 24 B include the cost of labels and indexes; treat the result as a floor [inference] and as a 2016 number.
"12 hours" is a "magic number" (note 50, p.98): enough information to debug an incident in RAM, with fast queries, without costing too much RAM. [from source] (SRE p.90, 98)

What leaves RAM: the in-memory state is periodically archived to the external TSDB (Time-Series Database) system; Borgmon can query it for older data, slower, but cheaper and larger than Borgmon's RAM. [from source] (SRE p.91)

At each interval Borgmon fetches /varz from each target, decodes it and stores it in memory; it spreads the collection of each instance across the interval, so targets do not run in lockstep. It writes synthetic variables per target (name resolved to host:port? answered the collection? answered the health check? when the collection finished?), which enables rules that detect unavailable tasks: the collection failure itself is a signal. Varz (HTTP) differs from SNMP, but experience shows this is rarely a problem (note 49). [from source] (SRE p.89-90) Scripts x common format (p.89): instead of running custom scripts to detect failures, Borgmon relies on a common data exposure format (white-box monitoring); this allows mass collection with low overhead and avoids the cost of running subprocesses and establishing network connections on every check; and, since collection does not happen in a short-lived process, the collected history also feeds the alert computation. Claiming that Borgmon "runs scripts per target" contradicts the book. [from source] (SRE p.89)

Mapped variable: http_responses map:code 200:25 404:0 500:12 = 25 responses with 200 and 12 responses with 500. Declaring a metric takes one line of code; the price of the schema-less interface is the maintenance of the rules (offset by tools that validate and generate rules). [from source] (SRE p.89)

Hierarchy that follows the service topology: typically one Borgmon per cluster and a pair at the global level; very large services shard below the cluster into "scraper" Borgmons that feed the cluster one. Between Borgmons a streaming protocol is used (saves CPU and network compared with varz text); two or more global ones give diversity in the face of maintenance and failures; the upper layers filter what they want to receive so as not to fill the arena with all per-task series. [from source] (SRE p.89, 95)

Borgmon is "a programmable calculator with syntactic sugar to generate alerts". Rules run in parallel in a threadpool, respecting order when a rule uses the output of another; the duration depends on the size of the vectors, so slowness is resolved with more CPU; rule execution time is exported ("monitoring the monitoring"). Aggregation is the cornerstone: summing the series of the tasks of a job to treat the job as a whole. [from source] (SRE p.92)

rate() returns the total delta divided by the total time between the first and last value in the window (e.g. [10m]); the window avoids missing points due to collection failure. The naming convention is the triplet level:variable:operation (e.g. task:http_requests:rate10m, dc:http_requests:rate10m). [from source] (SRE p.93)

Note 52 (p.98): computing the sum of rates (rate per task and then sum) instead of the rate of the sum protects the result against a counter reset or missing data, for example due to a task restart or failed collection. Note 53: although untyped, most varz are simple counters and the rate function handles all reset cases. Counters do not lose meaning when there are events between samplings; gauges may lose that activity (p.92). [from source]

Book example with 5 tasks (10-min rates in req/s: 1; 0.9; 1.1; 0; 1): the datacenter sum is 4 req/s. Errors (code 500): 0.6 req/s in total; error ratio = 0.6 ÷ 4 = 0.15 (15%). The alert rule requires ratio > 0.01 and errors > 1/s: the ratio is far above, but the 0.6 errors/s do not exceed 1/s, so the alert is not active; when it exceeds 1/s it stays pending for 2 minutes (for 2m) before firing. [from source] (SRE p.93-95; ratio calculation [derived])

Minimum duration: alerts "flap"; so the rule requires the condition to stay true for a minimum time, typically at least two rule evaluation cycles, so that a missed collection does not generate a false alert. [from source] (SRE p.94-95) The example threshold (1% and 1 error/s) is an illustration from the book, not a universal rule.

Firing sends an Alert RPC to Alertmanager (when the rule fires and again when it is considered "firing"), which routes: it can inhibit alerts when others are active, deduplicate across Borgmons with the same labelset and do fan-in/fan-out by labelset. Page alerts go to the on-call, important but subcritical ones to the ticket queue, the rest stays as information in status dashboards. [from source] (SRE p.95)

The Prober runs a protocol check against the target, validates the payload (for example the HTML), can extract values as series and export timing histograms by operation and payload size; pointed at the frontend domain and behind the balancer, it distinguishes a localized failure (one datacenter) and suppresses alerts. [from source] (SRE p.96)

Configuration separates rules from targets; there are templates (rule libraries) of two kinds: schema of variables exported by code libraries (HTTP server, memory allocator, storage client, RPC) and aggregation from the task up to the global service; unit and regression tests synthesize series; a continuous integration service runs the suite, packages and distributes the configuration, which each Borgmon validates before accepting. Groupings follow a shared destination (tasks by config files, jobs of a shard per datacenter, sites by network). [from source] (SRE p.96-97)

Chapter conclusion: the maintenance cost must grow sublinearly with the size of the service; decouple the size of the monitored system from the size of the rules. Open source tools with similar ideas: Prometheus, Riemann, Heka, Bosun. [from source] (SRE p.88, 97-98)
Post-blind-test correction (round 3): p.55 only appeared as a Here are the definitions, paraphrased.

Root cause: a defect in a software or human system that, if repaired, gives confidence that the event will not recur in the same way. The same incident can have several root causes; the book's example is the combination of insufficient process automation, software that crashed on invalid input and insufficient testing of the script that generates the configuration. Each of these factors could be a root cause on its own and each must be repaired. Note: in that definition the "software that crashed" is one of the root causes; it is not the "trigger", a concept that comes from the Appendix D template (p.334). (SRE p.55)
Push: any change to the running software of a service or to its configuration. (SRE p.55)
Alert: notification meant to be read by a person and pushed to a bug/ticket queue, an e-mail alias or a pager; they are classified, respectively, as tickets, email alerts and pages. (SRE p.55)

Node and machine: terms used interchangeably for a running kernel instance, on a physical server, a VM or a container. On the same machine there can coexist services related to each other (a cache server and a web server) or unrelated (a code repository and the master of a configuration system such as Puppet or Chef). (SRE p.55)

Monitoring is collecting, processing, aggregating and displaying quantitative data in real time (counts and types of queries, errors, processing times, server lifetime). White-box: metrics exposed by the interior of the system (logs, JVM profiling interface, an HTTP handler that emits internal statistics). Black-box: testing externally visible behavior, as a user would see it. Dashboard: an application (usually web) with the summarized view of the service's core metrics, pre-assembled, which can include ticket queue size, high-priority bugs, who is on-call and recent pushes. The book itself warns that there is no uniformly shared vocabulary, not even within Google; the definitions are the most common interpretations. (SRE p.55)
Note 25 (p.62): zero redundancy (N + 0) situations count as "imminent" for saturation purposes, as do "almost full" parts of the service. (SRE p.62)

Notes 45 and 46 (p.98): non-SRE teams often use a generator to create the initial boilerplate and the updates of alert rules and find it easier (though less powerful) than editing the rules directly; other applications also export their internal state through their own service protocol: OpenLDAP via the cn=Monitor subtree, MySQL with SHOW VARIABLES, Apache with the mod_status handler. (SRE p.98)

Notes 43 and 44 (p.98): note 43 (tied to the term varz, p.89) says the name is pronounced "var-zee", because Google was born in the US; note 44 says the plural of Borgmon is Borgmon itself, like "sheep", i.e. the spelling "Borgmen" is wrong. Whoever asks how varz is pronounced or what the plural of Borgmon is finds the answer in these two footnotes. [from source] (SRE p.98)

Burn-rate-based alerts; RED/USE; real overhead per series beyond the 24 B per point (labels, indexes) and sizing for other products (the book only gives the 17 GB example); modern distributed tracing/OpenTelemetry (only cites Dapper for tracing, p.107); P0/P1 levels; universal alert thresholds (only examples, such as error ratio >1% in 10 min and >1 error/s, p.95). For modern observability, refer to observability-opentelemetry-expert.
At most 50% on purely operational work; of the rest, at most 25% on-call. [from source] (SRE p.99-100)
Agreed response times: typically 5 min for user-facing or very sensitive services, 30 min for less sensitive ones. [from source] (SRE p.99)
99.99% in a quarter allows about 13 min of downtime, hence the on-call reaction in minutes. [from source] (SRE p.99-100)
Minimum of 8 engineers at a single site (2 people on-call, one-week shifts); in dual-site, 6 per site. Preference for multi-site (follow the sun). [from source] (SRE p.100)

Quality: on average 6 hours to handle an incident (analysis, remediation, follow-ups), hence a maximum of 2 incidents per 12 h shift; incident = events/alerts with the same root cause that would go into the same postmortem. [from source] (SRE p.100-101)
Compensation: time-off-in-lieu or money with a cap. [from source] (SRE p.101) [DATED]

Feeling safe: stress impairs cognition (e.g., confirmation bias, cited as an illustrative example of heuristics under stress); three resources: clear escalation paths, well-defined incident management procedures, a blameless postmortem culture. [from source] (SRE p.101)
The book does not turn this bias into a rule for investigating an external cause; using the example that way is [inference].

App. B (p.331), limit per shift [from source]: expect at most two events per on-call shift (for example, per 12 hours), because responding, fixing the outage, starting the postmortem and filing the bugs takes time; more events can degrade the quality of the response and suggest a problem in system design, monitoring sensitivity or the response to postmortem bugs (the same argument appears in the 6 h per incident arithmetic on p.101; more detail in gestao-treinamento-interrupts-e-engajamento.md). (SRE p.331; p.101)

Operational overload: measurable goals (e.g., daily tickets < 5; paging events per shift < 2); a common cause is badly configured monitoring; "give back the pager" in extreme cases. [from source] (SRE p.102-103)

Underload: system too quiet; size so that each engineer is on-call once or twice a quarter; "Wheel of Misfortune" exercises and the annual disaster recovery event DiRT (Disaster Recovery Training: theoretical and practical drills, multi-day tests) help keep skills practiced. P.331 (App. B) only brings the irony that good practices leave the team out of practice and asks for practicing hypothetical outages. [from source] (SRE p.103)
Hypothetico-deductive method: report → telemetry/logs → hypotheses → test (compare or "treat" the system) → cause → fix and postmortem. [from source] (SRE p.104)
Steps: Problem Report, Triage, Examine, Diagnose, Test and Treat, Cure. [from source] (SRE p.106-111)

Pitfalls: irrelevant symptoms, not knowing how to change the system safely, improbable or past-bound theories, spurious correlations ("horses, not zebras"). Correlation is not causation: the book's example is packet loss inside a cluster and hard drives failing in the cluster, correlated events that have a common cause, a power outage, even though a network failure obviously does not cause disk failure or vice versa; and, the larger the system and the more metrics, it is inevitable that some events correlate by pure coincidence. [from source] (SRE p.106)

Triage: respond proportionally to impact; in a severe outage the priority is to stop the bleeding (divert traffic, drop load, shut down subsystems) while preserving evidence; "fly the airplane" analogy. [from source] (SRE p.106-107)
Examine: metrics, logging (adjustable verbosity levels, sampling), tracing (Dapper), current-state endpoints. [from source] (SRE p.107)
Diagnose: simplify and reduce; divide and conquer/bisection; ask "what/where/why"; "what touched it last" (recent changes). [from source] (SRE p.108-109)
Test and Treat: tests with mutually exclusive alternatives, obvious first, attention to confounding factors and side effects; record everything. [from source] (SRE p.110)
Negative results are magic: negative results are conclusive and should be published. [from source] (SRE p.110-111)

App Engine case study: mitigated with resources before finding the cause (whitelist created on each access to a path, triggered by a security scanner); notes 75 and 76 are on p.115. [from source] (SRE p.112-115)
Making troubleshooting easier: white-box observability and structured logs from the start, request ID, changes recorded. [from source] (SRE p.114)

Three cases: Test-Induced (a test that blocked access to a DB and exposed dependencies), Change-Induced (a config push that caused a global crash loop and was rolled back in ~5 min), Process-Induced (turndown automation of small installations that sent to Diskerase the machines of all installations in turndown globally; the large installations were not affected, p.119). [from source] (SRE p.116-120)

Lessons, one per case: rollback must be tested before large-scale tests (Test-Induced, p.117); full canary "regardless of perceived risk" and the luck that the engineer who pushed was following real-time channels (Change-Induced, p.118); automation without sanity checks ("empty filter = all") is dangerous (Process-Induced, p.119-120). Details in the next section. [from source] (SRE p.117-120)
General: every problem has a solution; keep a history of outages; ask improbable questions ("what if"); encourage proactive testing; do not panic. [from source] (SRE p.116, 120-121)
Test-Induced (SRE p.116-117): the lesson is the tested rollback.
Change-Induced (SRE p.117-119): the lesson is the full canary and what was luck.
Process-Induced (SRE p.119-120): the lesson is validating the filter output (empty set).

Cause: the turndown server had no sanity checks; when run again and receiving an empty response for the rack, it passed the empty filter to the machine database, which ordered all of them wiped ("sometimes zero means everything"). Slow and unreliable reinstallation by TFTP at the lowest QoS from distant locations (BIOS hung or went into continuous reboot, depending on the network card), a regression that limited to at most two setup tasks per worker, poorly tuned QoS and timeouts, and forced kernel reinstallation; the solution was to reclassify installation traffic with slightly higher priority and restart machines stuck by automation. (SRE p.119-120)

General points of the chapter: "every problem has a solution"; if overloaded, call in more people (sometimes the whole company); "the one with the most state is often the one who triggered the event"; keep a history of outages and chase the follow-up of postmortems; ask the "what if" (building without power, racks in water, primary datacenter dark, compromised web server); test proactively with the best people nearby (not at 2 a.m. on Saturday). (SRE p.116, 120-121)

On-call: with 99.99% in the quarter the allowed downtime is ~13 minutes [derived: 0.0001 × 90 days × 1,440 min ≈ 13 min, the book says "around 13 minutes"], hence the reaction is "on the order of minutes"; incident = related events that fit in the same postmortem; an incident consumes on average 6 hours, which gives at most 2 per 12 h shift; tune toward a 1:1 alert/incident ratio; example goals for overload: daily tickets < 5 and page events per shift < 2. (SRE p.99-102)

Troubleshooting: logging with adjustable verbosity levels and sampling (e.g., record 1 in every 1,000 operations), request tracing through the stack with Dapper; Shakespeare probe example that runs every minute and, in a 10-minute window, about half of the probes work (indicates partial failure and not total); in the App Engine case, the extra latency came from a gap of ~250 ms between the start of work on a request and the first RPCs. (SRE p.107-113)
Three risks: narrow technical focus, poor communication, freelancing. [from source] (SRE p.122-123)

Based on the Incident Command System; four roles: Incident Command, Operational Work (Ops), Communication, Planning. Only the operations team modifies the system during the incident. [from source] (SRE p.123)

Elements: recursive separation of responsibilities, recognized command post, live incident state document, clear, live handoff ("You're now the incident commander, okay?" with confirmation). [from source] (SRE p.123-124)
When to declare an incident (any one true): needs a second team; customer-visible outage; no solution after an hour of focused analysis. [from source] (SRE p.125)
Best practices: Prioritize, Prepare, Trust, Introspect, Consider alternatives, Practice, Change it around. [from source] (SRE p.125)

Fields in order: title with date and link to cheat sheet (the example's header says the Communications lead keeps the Summary up to date); Summary; Status (incident #465); Command Post(s); Command Hierarchy (IC, Operations lead, Planning lead, Communications lead, next IC — update at least every 4 hours and on Comms handoff); Detailed Status; Exit Criteria (e.g., availability and latency SLOs for 30+ minutes); TODO list and bugs filed; Incident timeline (most recent first, UTC). [from source] (SRE p.332-333)

The example is the same incident #465 of Shakespeare Sonnet++ from App. D: status active, command post in #shakespeare on IRC, IC jennifer (who also covers Planning and Comms), Ops docbrown, last update at 15:28 UTC; the example's exit criteria: new sonnet in the corpus and 99.99% availability with p99 latency < 100 ms for more than 30 minutes; TODOs: reindex (done), borrow emergency capacity (done), enable the "flux capacitor" (bug 5554823, pending); timeline entries: 14:55 pager storm, 15:01 incident declared, 15:04 sonnet text obtained from the shakespeare-discuss@ list, 15:10 sonnet added and index MapReduce started, 15:21 all traffic to USA-2 ("sacrificial cluster") and draining of the others, 15:28 global capacity increase of 2x. The full narrative and the outcome (10x, return at 1/10/30/50/100%, end at 16:30 after 30 nominal min) are in postmortem-e-rastreamento-de-outages.md. [from source] (SRE p.332-335)

The distribution of roles between primary and secondary varies: one team uses the secondary as a fall-through for pages the primary misses; another leaves the primary with only pages and the secondary with the rest of the non-urgent activities. When they do not need an exclusive secondary rotation, two related teams can serve as each other's secondary. Pages take priority over almost everything, including projects; non-page events (lower-priority alerts, releases) can be handled during business hours. Google delivers pages by multiple means (email, SMS, robot call, app) on several devices. (SRE p.99-100)

On-call quality: the distribution of page events should be very flat, with a likely median of 0; if a component pages every day (median incidents/day > 1) it is likely that something else will break and blow the limit; if the limit is temporarily exceeded (for example in a quarter), corrective measures should return the load to a sustainable state. Multi-site brings communication and coordination cost: the single/multi-site decision weighs trade-offs, the importance of the system and the load. Night shifts harm health; limiting the size of the rotation avoids losing touch with production. (SRE p.100-101)

Feeling safe: two ways of thinking (intuitive and fast versus rational and deliberate); under stress (cortisol, CRH) the second tends to be swallowed by the first and the on-call abuses heuristics, e.g., confirmation bias when the same alert pages for the fourth time in the week and the three previous ones came from an external infrastructure system (this is the book's illustrative example of how stress leads to automatically associating the fourth occurrence with the previous cause; it is not the book's recommendation on how to handle an external cause: the book gives no specific guidance for that case); intuition may be wrong and habitual quick reactions can be disastrous. The developers of the teams SRE supports also participate in a 24/7 rotation, and one can always escalate to them. When the incident is complex enough to involve several teams, or an upper bound on its duration cannot be estimated, it is advisable to adopt the formal incident management protocol, supported at Google by a web tool that automates handover of roles and status recording/communication (so as not to spend effort formatting emails). (SRE p.101-102)

Overload: page alerts should be aligned with symptoms that threaten the SLO and be actionable; low-priority alerts that bother every hour create fatigue and make serious alerts get less attention; the alert fan-out per incident should be regulated by grouping related alerts and silencing duplicate or uninformative ones; noisy alerts should be tuned toward a 1:1 ratio. If the change causing the overload comes from the developers, set common goals with them; as a last resort, "give back the pager" (the development team is exclusively on call until the system reaches the standard), which is rare; temporary alternative: renegotiate to route some or all pages to the developers' on-call until the service can be taken back. (SRE p.102-103)

Effective problem report: expected behavior, actual behavior and, if possible, how to reproduce; consistent form and searchable storage (bug system); teams have forms or small web apps that generate and route the bug automatically and may offer self-diagnosis. It is practice to open a bug for each problem, even one received by email or chat; many teams discourage reporting directly to a person (requires transcribing, produces worse reports invisible to the team, concentrates the load on whoever the reporter knows rather than on the on-call). (SRE p.106)

Shakespeare example: the black-box prober looks for "the forms of things unknown" and the alert already opens a bug with links to the results and the playbook; the prober does a GET on /api/search and expects HTTP 200 with an exact JSON; it probes every minute and, in 10 minutes, about half succeeded with no pattern; the prober does not show what came back in the failures (note it to fix); with curl one gets a 502 with no payload, but with the X-Request-Trace header listing the backends involved, which rules out the frontend and the load balancers as the source. (SRE p.106-109)

Diagnose: injecting known test data at each step (black-box) and having a reproducible test case speeds everything up and allows using a non-production environment with more invasive techniques; divide and conquer from one end to the other (good for pipelines) or bisection in huge systems. "What, where, why" example (Spanner with high latency: CPU in the tasks; profiling shows log sorting; the cost is in a regex; solution: rewrite to avoid backtracking, look for similar patterns, consider RE2, which does not backtrack and has linear growth, while PCRE can take exponential time, note 68). "What touched it last": systems have inertia; mark the start and end of deploys on the error graphs. (SRE p.108-109)

Test and Treat: five cautions when designing tests: mutually exclusive alternatives; obvious first, in decreasing order of likelihood and considering the risk; confounding factors (a firewall rule that only allows a certain IP); side effects of active tests (more CPUs can increase data races; verbose logging can worsen a latency problem); some tests only suggest (race conditions and deadlocks that are hard to reproduce). Write down ideas, tests and results; in a shared document or chat, the timestamp helps the postmortem and informs others (note 70); record changes systematically so they can be undone. (SRE p.110, 115)

"Negative results are magic": negative results are conclusive (one example: a web server handled only ~800 of the 8,000 connections needed due to lock contention, and that record saves the next team the experiment); microbenchmarks, documented antipatterns and project postmortems qualify; benchmark tools and load generators can be born from experiments that did not confirm (Apache Bench); publishing improves the data-based culture; be suspicious of a document that mentions no failure. (SRE p.110-111)

Cure: proving the cause in production is hard because systems are complex (several factors that together cause it, path/state dependence) and reproducing may be infeasible; a non-production environment mitigates, at the cost of maintaining another copy of the system; afterward, write the postmortem. (SRE p.111)

App Engine case study (simplified version): latency rose almost an order of magnitude, CPU and processes nearly quadrupled, with no traffic increase and no code or infrastructure change (the change was on a Saturday, with no pushes underway); other apps were not affected; the correlation with merge_join (suspected index) was spurious because even static content, served without the datastore, was slow; there were ~250 ms between the start of work on the request and the first RPCs, where Dapper does not help because it only traces RPCs; since the customer had a public launch the following week, they mitigated before understanding, recommending the instance type with more CPU, which brought latency to an acceptable level; the root cause: an old access-control bug created a whitelist object every time a specific path was accessed, and an automatic security scanner generated thousands of objects in half an hour, which came to be checked on every request (common pattern: configuration objects read from the datastore and kept in memory, with time proportional to the quantity, note 76). Note 75 (printed on p.115 of the PDF) admits that launching with an unidentified bug is not ideal, but eliminating all known bugs is usually impractical. (SRE p.112-115)

Troubleshooting notes (p.114-115): "horses, not zebras" holds in some domains, but in a system with a well-designed cluster filesystem entire classes of failure can be eliminated (note 61); prefer simple explanations, but remember Hickam's dictum (several small problems can explain all the symptoms, note 62); the 5 Whys technique (Ohno) resembles "what, where, why" (note 67); note 72 refers to works on the limits of looking for a single root cause. To make troubleshooting easier: white-box observability and structured logs from the start, well-understood interfaces between components and a unique request ID across RPCs. (SRE p.114-115)

The book's unmanaged incident (Mary, 2 p.m. on a Thursday): three of five datacenters go down in sequence and the rest overload; Mary looks at logs, reverts the release with no effect, calls whoever wrote the code (3:30 a.m. in their time zone), other colleagues "just look", executives and vice presidents demand an ETA and make irrelevant suggestions, and Malcolm, uncoordinated, deploys a CPU affinity change that takes down the servers. Hazards: narrow technical focus, poor communication and freelancing. (SRE p.122-123)

Roles (p.123): the *incident commander* holds the high-level state, structures the task force and in fact fills all the roles not delegated; the *Ops lead* applies the operational tools and only the operations team modifies the system; *Communication* is the public face, issues periodic updates to the team and stakeholders (usually by email) and may keep the incident document up to date; *Planning* handles the longer term: filing bugs, ordering dinner, organizing handoffs and tracking how far the system has diverged from normal so it can be reverted later. If someone's load is excessive, ask the planning lead for more people and delegate, including creating sub-incidents. The clear separation of responsibilities gives more autonomy, since no one needs to doubt a colleague. (SRE p.123)

Command post (p.123-124): war room or working at desks with email and IRC; Google considers IRC a great help (reliable, serves as a log of communications, bots record incident traffic and events such as alerts, useful for distributed teams). The live incident state document is the IC's most important responsibility: editable by several people (most use Google Docs; Google Docs SRE uses Google Sites, since depending on the software you are trying to fix is a bad idea); it can be messy, but must be functional; use a template and the most important information at the top; keep it for the postmortem. Handoff: at the end of the day, pass command explicitly (by phone or video, saying "you're now the incident commander, okay?") and only leave the call with a firm acceptance; tell everyone who is leading. (SRE p.124)

Managed incident: Mary hands command to Sabrina, who summarizes by email to a pre-agreed list, records the impact assessment, keeps VPs informed without minutiae, asks an external communications representative to draft the message to users, and calls in the on-call developer only with Mary's approval; those helping prioritize the delegated tasks and report what they do; at 5 p.m. she starts finding replacements, at 5:45 p.m. there is a conference, at 6 p.m. the handoff to the sister office, which mitigates, closes and starts the postmortem. (SRE p.124)

Declare early (p.125): it is better to declare the incident early and close it with a simple fix than to trigger the framework hours later. Skills atrophy without use: use the framework in ordinary operational changes that cross time zones/teams, include incident management in disaster recovery tests (DiRT) and simulate responses to problems already solved. Stated result: lower mean time to recovery and less stressful work. Best practices: Prioritize (stop the bleeding, restore service, preserve evidence), Prepare, Trust (autonomy within the role), Introspect (attention to emotional state; if you panic, ask for support), Consider alternatives, Practice, Change it around (switch roles). (SRE p.125)

What the book says about compensation (p.101). One must consider adequate compensation for out-of-hours support; organizations handle this in different ways, and Google offers time off in lieu (time-off-in-lieu) or cash payment, with a cap defined as some proportion of total salary. (SRE p.101)

What the cap is for (p.101). The compensation cap represents, in practice, a limit on the amount of on-call work any person will take on. The structure ensures the incentive to take part in on-call as the team needs, but also promotes balanced distribution of on-call and limits the possible negative effects of too much on-call, such as burnout or lack of time for projects. (SRE p.101)

How it fits with the rest of the chapter (p.100). Google's ideal is to invest at least 50% of SRE time in engineering; of the rest, at most 25% on-call, leaving up to another 25% for other operational non-project work; the 25% rule gives the minimum of 8 SREs for a 24/7 rotation at a single site (primary and secondary, weekly shifts, each person on-call one week per month) and 6 per team at two sites. There are at most 2 incidents per 12-hour shift (p.101). That is, the compensation cap is a second brake on the same sustainability problem. (SRE p.100-101)

The book does not state the percentage of salary used as the cap nor time-off amounts per on-call hour; nor does it address the labor law regime on standby duty of any country. Any number, article of law or standby rule (for example in Brazil) is outside the book and, from memory, is [extrapolation]: the correct conduct is to refer to legal or HR instead of quoting values.
Severity levels (SEV); "scribe" or "liaison" roles; standard status cadence beyond the 4 h of the example; MTTD; runbooks as a separate document (it uses "playbook").
Postmortem = a written record of an incident: impact, mitigation/resolution actions, root cause(s) and follow-up actions to prevent recurrence. [from source] (SRE p.126)

Write a postmortem for all significant incidents, whether or not they generated a page; those that did NOT generate a page are even more valuable, since they probably point to clear monitoring gaps. Google operates in a blameless postmortem culture. [from source] (SRE p.25)
Goals: incident documented, contributing root causes well understood, effective preventive actions. [from source] (SRE p.126)

Common triggers (define before the incident; any stakeholder can request one): downtime/degradation above a threshold; data loss; on-call intervention (rollback, rerouting); resolution time above a threshold; monitoring failure. [from source] (SRE p.126)

Blameless: assume good intent and the information available; focus on systemic reasons; "you can't fix people, but you can fix systems and processes". Blaming leads to hiding problems. [from source] (SRE p.126-127)
Desirable writing tool: real-time collaboration, open commenting, email notifications. [from source] (SRE p.127)
Formal review criteria (5): key data collected, complete impact, root cause deep enough, appropriate action plan with priority, outcome shared with stakeholders. [from source] (SRE p.127)
"No postmortem left unreviewed"; repository of past incidents. [from source] (SRE p.128)

Dissemination: postmortem of the month, reading clubs, Wheel of Misfortune, discussion group. Publicly reward those who do the right thing (peer bonus). Ask for feedback on effectiveness (toil of writing?). [from source] (SRE p.128-129)
Privacy: no information that identifies an end user in postmortems. [from source] (text on p.127; note 80 is on PDF page 129) (SRE p.127, 129)
Caveat: Ch. 15 does not list the template fields; it refers to Appendix D. [from source] (SRE p.127)

Fields in order: Date; Authors; Status; Summary; Impact; Root Causes (note suggests 5 Whys); Trigger; Resolution; Detection; Action Items; Lessons Learned (What went well, What went wrong, Where we got lucky); Timeline; Supporting information. [from source] (SRE p.334-336)
Two distinct durations: OUTAGE (14:54-16:00, 66 min) and INCIDENT (15:01-16:30). The 66 minutes are in the Summary (p.334); the times are in the timeline (p.335). [from source] (SRE p.334-335)
The example's action list includes freezing production due to error budget exhaustion. [from source] (SRE p.334)

The Action Items table in App. D is cut off at the right margin of the PDF: only the "Action Item" column is legible (SRE p.334); it is not known whether there were owner or deadline columns. Owners appear as TODO(name) in the App. F minutes (SRE p.340).
An owner/deadline per action is good practice [extrapolation].

Header. Summary: Shakespeare Search was down for 66 minutes during a period of very high interest because of the discovery of a new sonnet. Impact: estimated 1.21 billion queries lost, no revenue impact; note 163 (p.336) defines Impact as the effect on users, revenue etc. Status: complete, actions in progress. (SRE p.334)

Root cause (note 164 suggests the 5 Whys technique): cascading failure from the combination of exceptional load with a resource leak (file descriptor exhaustion, according to the logs) that occurred when a search failed because the term was not in the corpus. The new sonnet used a word that had never appeared in a work of Shakespeare's and that was precisely the term users were searching for. Under normal conditions the failure rate from this leak is low enough to go unnoticed. Trigger: latent bug triggered by a sudden traffic increase. (SRE p.334-335)

Resolution: traffic directed to the sacrificial cluster and 10x capacity to contain the cascade; updated index deployed, resolving the interaction with the latent bug; extra capacity kept until public interest dropped; leak identified and fix deployed. Detection: Borgmon detected many HTTP 500s and paged the on-call. (SRE p.334)

Actions (9 legible items): update the playbook for cascades; use the "flux capacitor" to balance load between clusters; schedule a cascade test in the next DiRT; investigate running the MapReduce/index merge continuously; plug the file descriptor leak in ranking; add load shedding; create regression tests for queries of death; deploy the fixed ranking; freeze production until 11/20/2015 due to error budget exhaustion, or request an exception (text cut off in the PDF). Note 165 warns that "reflex" actions are usually extreme or expensive and that there is a risk of over-optimizing for one problem (e.g., creating a specific alert when unit tests would catch the error much earlier). (SRE p.334, 336)

Lessons: what went well: monitoring alerted quickly on the HTTP 500 rate (near 100%); the updated corpus was distributed quickly to all clusters. What went wrong: the team was out of practice responding to a cascade; the error budget was exceeded by several orders of magnitude because the traffic spike resulted almost entirely in failure. Luck: there was a list of enthusiasts with the text of the sonnet; the server logs had stack traces pointing to the file descriptor exhaustion; the query of death was resolved by pushing an index that contained the popular term. Note 166 says "Where we got lucky" is for near misses (SRE p.335-336).

Timeline (note 167 calls it the "script of the incident" and says to start from the incident management document's timeline): 14:51 news of the sonnet; 14:53 Shakespeare Search traffic rises 88x (a post on /r/shakespeare points to the search engine as the place for the sonnet, which was not even in the corpus yet); 14:54 OUTAGE begins (backends melting); 14:55 pager storm (ManyHttp500s in all clusters); 14:57 all traffic failing; 14:58 the on-call (docbrown) investigates, very high crash rate; 15:01 INCIDENT begins: incident #465 declared, coordination in #shakespeare, jennifer named incident commander; 15:03 incident list notified; 15:04-15:10 sonnet text located, corpus update documentation found, sonnet added and indexing started; 15:06 identical symptoms in all clusters; 15:12 two devs called; 15:18 "smoking gun" in the logs: file descriptor exhaustion, confirmed in the code (leak if the term is not in the corpus); 15:20 index MapReduce finishes; 15:21 decision to increase instances enough that each instance does useful work before dying and restarting; 15:23 all traffic to the USA-2 cluster (sacrificial), freeing the instance increase in the other clusters without the servers failing immediately; 15:25 replication of the new index; 15:28 2x increase of instances begins; 15:32 balancing goes back to increasing traffic to non-sacrificial clusters; 15:33 the tasks in the non-sacrificial clusters fail again, same symptoms; 15:34 order-of-magnitude error discovered in the whiteboard math for the instance increase; 15:36 balancing goes back to sacrificing USA-2 to prepare another global 5x increase (total 10x the initial capacity) and OUTAGE MITIGATED (updated index replicated to all clusters); 15:39 second wave of increase up to 10x; gradual return of traffic: 15:41 1%, 15:43 nominal HTTP 500 rate and intermittent task failures at a low level, 15:45 10%, 15:47 within SLO with no task failures, 15:50 30%, 15:55 50%, 16:00 OUTAGE ends with all traffic balanced across all clusters; 16:30 INCIDENT ends, exit criterion of 30 minutes of nominal performance reached. (SRE p.335)

App. C (incident state document, p.332-333) follows the same story: active status, command post in #shakespeare on IRC; hierarchy (IC jennifer; Ops docbrown; Planning and Comms also jennifer; next IC to be defined, update at least every 4 hours and on the Comms lead change); exit criteria: sonnet in the corpus and 99.99% availability with p99 latency < 100 ms for more than 30 minutes; TODOs: reindex (done), borrow emergency capacity (done), turn on the flux capacitor (bug 5554823, pending); timeline from most recent to oldest, with the same sequence (15:28 +2x; 15:21 everything to USA-2 "sacrificial cluster" and draining the others so they recover while more tasks come up). App. C marks 15:21 and App. D marks 15:23 for the diversion to USA-2: the book itself has a 2-minute discrepancy. (SRE p.332-333, 335)

1.21 billion / 66 min ≈ 18.3 million queries lost per minute (simple average, assumes a uniform rate; the book does not give this number). The book does not say how many instances were the "initial" ones nor the numeric value of the math error beyond "order of magnitude"; the jump from 2x to 10x is what the timeline shows (15:28 2x;

Useful patterns from the case: (a) sacrificial cluster = concentrate traffic on one cluster so the others recover and receive capacity before reintroducing load (p.332, 335); (b) reintroduce traffic in steps (1%, 10%, 30%, 50%, 100%) watching the error rate and task failures at each step (p.335); (c) exit criterion by time of nominal performance (30 min) instead of "looks resolved" (p.332, 335);
(d) the capacity calculation done on a whiteboard failed by an order of magnitude: recheck emergency calculations (p.335, lesson [inference]).
Postmortems cover only large incidents; aggregated data answers: how many alerts per shift, actionable/non-actionable ratio, which service generates the most toil. [from source] (SRE p.130)
Escalator tracks the acknowledgement and escalates if nobody acknowledges; Outalator groups alerts into incidents, keeps annotations and allows statistics. [from source] (SRE p.130-131)
Hierarchical colon tagging (cause:network:switch), "bogus" tag for false positives; free tags avoid a fixed list. [from source] (SRE p.131-133)

Tags with typos (the book's example is "cause:netwrok") and not very useful tags ("problem-went-away") exist and are accepted: the book says that avoiding a predetermined list and letting each team find its own preferences and patterns results in a more useful tool and better data; the tags were "remarkably powerful" for seeing a service's pain points even with little or no formal analysis. [from source] (SRE p.131, 133)
The book does not propose normalizing or fixing tags; any normalization routine is [extrapolation].

"Building your own Outalator": messaging systems such as Slack, Hipchat or IRC, used for internal communication and updating status dashboards, are good integration points for a system like this. This is the only mention of Slack as a tool (the other occurrences of the word in the book are "slack capacity" and "slack CPU", spare capacity, a different topic). [from source] (SRE p.131)
Analysis: basic counts, comparisons between teams and over time, semantic patterns; the number of incidents does not indicate severity or difficulty. [from source] (SRE p.133-134)

Unexpected uses: "dummy escalator" (configuration with no human recipient; notifications appear in the Outalator and can be tagged, annotated and reviewed) to record and audit the use of privileged or role accounts and to annotate runs of periodic jobs that are possibly not idempotent (e.g., applying schema changes from version control). The book caveats that the functionality is basic and serves technical, not legal audits: it does not claim legal or compliance value for this trail. [from source] (SRE p.133)

More details from Ch. 16: Escalator was conceived as a nearly transparent tool that received copies of the emails sent to on-call aliases, without changing the behavior of whoever alerts (p.130); Outalator shows the queues of several teams interleaved in time and keeps a copy of the original notification and of the email replies; annotations can be marked "important" (the other parts of the message are collapsed) (p.130); alerts grouped into an incident allow analyzing "incidents per day" separately from "alerts per day" (p.131); one event usually triggers several alerts (e.g., a network failure notifies all teams, including the NOC) and reducing alerts per event is desirable but there is always a trade-off between false positives and false negatives (p.131); colon tags form namespaces (cause:network:switch vs cause:network:cable; suggested prefixes "cause" and "action", derived from each team's historical use); "bogus" for false positives; tags such as "customer:132456" become links (p.131-133). Analysis layers: basic counts (incidents per week/month/quarter, alerts per incident); comparison between teams and over time ("it's the third this week" only makes sense knowing whether before it was 5 per day or 5 per month); semantic analysis (component that causes the most incidents; note 85: "more incidents" may be an artifact of over-sensitive monitoring, and the number of incidents measures neither severity nor difficulty) (p.133-134). The shift handoff report and the "report mode" for the weekly production reviews use the important annotations (p.133). Non-obvious benefit: seeing that a dependency team (e.g., Bigtable) was not alerted and notifying it manually (p.133). [from source]

[from source] (SRE p.339-340)

Content of Resources in the example minutes: resources borrowed to respond to the sonnet++ incident, with extra instances to shut down and resources to return the following week; utilization at 60% CPU, 75% RAM and 44% disk (up from 40%, 70% and 40% the previous week). The action items "raise the AnnotationConsistencyTooEventual threshold" and "return the instance count to normal and return the resources" are in New Action Items, not in Resources. [from source] (SRE p.340)

Why it exists: without formally learning from incidents, they may repeat "ad infinitum" and multiply in complexity or cascade; the chapter provides criteria for when to write one, practices and advice for cultivating the culture. Writing the postmortem is not punishment, it is a learning opportunity for the whole company; there is a cost in time and effort, so one is deliberate about when to write (the objective triggers on p.126 plus any stakeholder's request). A detailed analysis of root cause analysis techniques is beyond scope; each team chooses the appropriate technique (p.126).

Blameless in practice (p.127): the culture originated in healthcare and aviation (where mistakes can be fatal); the focus becomes why a person or team had incomplete or incorrect information. Book example: "finger pointing" ("we need to rewrite the entire complicated backend... if I get paged one more time, I'll rewrite it myself") versus "blameless" (an action to rewrite the backend might prevent these pages, the manual for this version is long and hard to train on; future on-calls will thank you). Removing blame gives confidence to escalate problems; one should also not stigmatize those who produce postmortems frequently, since an atmosphere of blame leads to hiding incidents. (SRE p.127)

Flow (p.127-128): the tool should have real-time collaboration, open commenting and email notifications; the draft circulates internally and a group of senior engineers assesses completeness with five questions (key data collected? complete impact? root cause deep enough? action plan and bug priority appropriate? outcome shared with stakeholders?); then it is disseminated to the widest possible audience; nothing that identifies an end user (note 80). "No postmortem left unreviewed": regular review sessions close discussions, capture ideas and finalize the state; then it goes to a repository of past incidents (note 81, printed on PDF page 129: Etsy released Morgue, a tool for managing postmortems). (SRE p.127-129)

Introducing the culture (p.128-129): active participation of senior management, but ideally it is the fruit of the engineers' self-motivation. Activities: postmortem of the month (newsletter), discussion group (Google+), reading clubs (sometimes of postmortems that are months or years old), Wheel of Misfortune (an old postmortem is re-enacted, with the original incident commander present). Against the cost objection: introduce gradually with a trial period (several complete and successful postmortems, which also help define the triggers); reward and celebrate the practice (publicly and in performance management); seek leadership support. The team is also surveyed on the effectiveness of the process (does the culture help? does writing involve much toil? what tools are missing?). (SRE p.128-129)

Example: at the 2014 TGIF, "The Art of the Postmortem", an SRE told how a freshly pushed release, despite being tested, took down a critical service for four minutes, and that it only lasted that long because he rolled back immediately; he received two peer bonuses (note 82 describes Google's Peer Bonus program as a way for colleagues to recognize exceptional effort, with a token cash reward; the book does NOT state the amount) and a big round of applause.

Today (p.129): it is a cultural norm that every significant incident has a complete postmortem; the "Postmortems at Google" working group coordinates templates, automates creation with data from the incident tools and extraction for trend analysis; the template gained additional metadata fields, without listing them; App. D is an example postmortem, not the list of those fields; future work: machine learning to predict weaknesses and reduce duplicate incidents. (SRE p.129)

CAPA and blameless postmortem in other industries (p.319): *corrective and preventative action* is the well-known concept of systematically investigating root causes to prevent recurrence and corresponds to SRE's blameless postmortem culture. What is assessed: what happened, the effectiveness of the response, what would be done differently next time and which actions will prevent repetition, without pointing at individuals; postmortems are done after incidents and published among the SRE teams so that everyone learns. (SRE p.319)

App. D notes (p.336): note 164 suggests the 5 Whys technique for understanding contributing factors; 165 says "reflex" actions are often extreme or expensive and there is a risk of over-optimizing for one problem (for example, creating specific monitoring when unit tests would catch the error earlier); 166 that "Where we got lucky" is for near misses, with the example of goat teleportation available for emergency use with other animals despite the lack of certification; 167 that the timeline is a "script" of the incident, filled in from the timeline of the incident management document and supplemented. All the App. D footnotes (163-168) are on p.336: 163 defines Impact as the effect on users, revenue etc.; 168 says "Supporting information" gathers useful information, links, logs, screenshots, graphs and IRC/IM logs. (SRE p.336)

What p.127-128 support. Blameless culture originated in healthcare and aviation; the blameless postmortem does not complain by pointing fingers, but points out where and how services can improve (book example: "we need to rewrite the whole backend!" × "an action item to rewrite the backend might prevent these pages and the manual for this version is long"); avoiding blame and keeping a constructive tone gives people confidence to escalate problems; do not stigmatize those who produce many postmortems; real-time collaboration, open commenting and email notifications; formal review by seniors with criteria (key data collected, complete impact, deep root cause, action plan and priority, outcome shared with those involved); no postmortem without review (p.128). (SRE p.127-128)

What they do not support. The texts deal with the postmortem document and the process around it; they are not a guide to the tone of chat conversations, team emails or review comments on releases and alerts. For giving feedback constructively to a team (explaining the reasoning and asking guiding, not loaded, questions), the book's basis is Ch. 30 (p.292-293); see gestao-treinamento-interrupts-e-engajamento.md. (SRE p.127-128, 292-293)

The duration in minutes of third-party incidents cited in other chapters (see Knight Capital in toil-automacao-e-simplicidade.md); how many instances were Shakespeare's "initial" capacity in App. D, the exact whiteboard calculation that was off by an order of magnitude and why the error occurred (the timeline only records the discovery at 15:34); Deadline for publishing a postmortem; numeric trigger thresholds; severity; MTTD; "just culture" by name; who approves the postmortem beyond "senior engineers" (SRE p.127).
SRE is Google's name for the discipline that covers a service's entire lifecycle: conception, deployment, operation, refinement and decommissioning. [from source] (SRE p.15)
Cited estimate: 40-90% of a system's total cost occurs after deployment; therefore software engineering "only up to birth" is the wrong view. [from source] (SRE p.15)
Reliability is the most fundamental feature; invest in it only up to the "reliable enough" point; after that the effort goes to features. [from source] (SRE p.15)
Author's definition: SRE is what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team. [from source] (SRE p.23)

SRE vs DevOps: the book says the principles are consistent; DevOps can be seen as a generalization of SRE principles, and SRE as a specific implementation of DevOps with its own extensions; Preface note 4 (p.20) says SRE is *distinct from the term DevOps* by its primary focus on reliability and its orientation toward removing the need for operations; that note supports the difference in focus, not a rivalry (the compatibility is in the box on p.24). [from source] (SRE p.24; note 4, p.20)

Direct cost: the team grows with the load because it depends on manual intervention. Indirect cost (larger): dev and ops have different vocabulary, incentives and stability goals, and the split degenerates into friction. [from source] (SRE p.22)
"Trench warfare" anti-pattern: ops creates launch gates and checklists; dev reacts by fragmenting changes (flag flips, cherrypicks) to escape review. [from source] (SRE p.23)

The book describes 50-60% Software Engineers and 40-50% candidates with 85-99% of the SWE profile plus rare knowledge (UNIX internals, layer 1-3 networking). [from source] (SRE p.23) [DATED] (Google's proportions in 2016)
Ceiling of 50% of aggregate time on "ops" work (tickets, on-call, manual tasks); below 50% on development, return the load to dev or hire without assigning extra ops. [from source] (SRE p.23-24)

Advantages: fast innovation, cheap teams, SREs grow sublinearly with the system. Challenges: hard hiring and the need for strong management support (e.g., stopping releases for the quarter when the error budget runs out). [from source] (SRE p.24)
availability, latency, performance, efficiency, change management, monitoring, emergency response, capacity planning. [from source] (SRE p.24)
Durable focus on engineering: monitor the operational load and redirect the excess (bugs/tickets) to development until it is back to ≤50%. [from source] (SRE p.24)
On-call: on average at most 2 events per 8-12 h shift; more causes fatigue, fewer wastes time. [from source] (SRE p.25)
Postmortems for all significant incidents, whether or not they paged; blame-free. [from source] (SRE p.25)
Error budget: 100% is the wrong target for almost everything; budget = 1 − availability target; set by the product. [from source] (SRE p.25)

Monitoring: valid outputs are alert, ticket and logging; requiring a human to read email to decide whether there is an action is "fundamentally flawed" (software interprets, humans are only notified when they need to act). [from source] (SRE p.25-26; reinforced in App. B, p.330)

Emergency: reliability depends on MTTF and MTTR; to assess the effectiveness of emergency response, the book says the most relevant metric is MTTR (how quickly the system is returned to health); "humans add latency": a system that avoids emergencies with human intervention has more availability; a playbook gives about 3x improvement in MTTR according to the book; "Wheel of Misfortune" is cited as training (p.26 only cites it; the postmortem re-enactment is on p.128, the description in Ch. 28, p.280, and the Wheel of Misfortune + DiRT pair appears on p.103). [from source] (SRE p.26)

Origin of the hierarchy: the book says it had not been explicitly developed until some Google SREs, among them former colleague Mikey Dickerson (note 41), temporarily joined the US government to help with the launch of healthcare.gov, in late 2013 and early 2014; they needed a way to explain how to increase the reliability of systems. Monitoring (base): without monitoring there is no way to know whether the service works ("flying blind"); you want to know about problems before the users do. [from source] (SRE p.85)

Incident Response: on-call is a tool for the larger mission and for staying in touch with how distributed systems work and fail, and Google would get rid of the pager if it could. "Making the problem go away" is not necessarily fixing it for good: you can stop the bleeding by reducing the system's precision, temporarily turning off features (graceful degradation) or diverting traffic to another healthy instance; the details depend on the service, but responding well to incidents applies to every team. Finding out what is wrong is the first step (structured troubleshooting); during the incident it is tempting to give in to adrenaline and act ad hoc, and the book advises against that; managing incidents well reduces impact and anxiety. [from source] (SRE p.85)

Postmortem and RCA: the goal is to be alerted and act manually only on new problems; "fixing" the same thing repeatedly is tedious and this way of thinking sets the SRE philosophy apart from more traditional operations environments. Blameless postmortem culture is the first step to understanding what went wrong (and what went right); the outage tracker records recent incidents, causes and actions (p.87). Themes: disaster preparation and testing, postmortem culture, automation and overhead reduction, structured and rational decision-making. Strategies seen outside Google: organizational focus on safety, attention to detail, swing capacity (telecom uses the "switch on wheels", a mobile telco office, for predictable events such as the Olympics), live simulations and drills, training and certification, detailed requirements gathering and defense in depth. Examples: nuclear Navy with real drills "weekly, two to three days a week"; lifeguards with a "mystery shopper" (staged drowning); defense: one year of design and three weeks of code; refinery/manufacturing: the former CEO of Alcoa required notification within 24 hours of any injury that cost a day of work; near misses treated as a preventive postmortem (CHIRP in the United Kingdom). (SRE p.318-320)

Automation (SRE p.320-321): the nuclear Navy (per the interviewee) avoided automation in favor of interlocks and procedures; trading became cautious (Knight Capital: US$ 440 million in a few hours, 2012; Flash Crash of 2010: trillions in 30 minutes); in the UK nuclear industry the rule of thumb is that if the plant must respond to a situation in less than 30 minutes, the response must be automated; in aviation the operational failover is automatic, but for some tasks automation is only trusted if verified by a human; in LASIK surgery automatic sanity checks on the entered data and automatic iris matching eliminated a class of medical errors.

Decision (SRE p.321-322): decision basis agreed in advance, clear inputs, explicit assumptions, data beats the opinion of the most senior person (HiPPO); trading separates an enforcement team that can shut the system down ("if we're not trading, we're not losing money") and only it turns it back on; telecom still uses long-distance switches from the 1980s ("bulletproof and massively redundant"); nuclear: "if it works now, don't touch it"; several industries rely on playbooks and procedures in which every conceivable scenario is in a checklist or in "the binder", the authoritative source of how to react, which suits slowly evolving industries or those with a limited-skill workforce (SRE p.322). Chapter conclusion: Google has a greater appetite for speed and, since lives are generally not at risk, uses error budgets to "fund" innovation (SRE p.322).

Ch. 34 (p.324-325): SRE went from a few hundred (2006) to more than 1,000 people at a dozen sites; airplane analogy: the cockpit of a 747 still has two pilots because the interfaces are well thought out; compact SRE team, at a high level of abstraction, with backup systems and deep knowledge coming from daily operations.

Time split and evolution of activities (Ch. 34, p.324-325). Teams are put together so that engineers split their time between two equally important kinds of work: (1) on-call, which is getting hands on the systems, seeing where and how they break and understanding scale challenges; (2) having time afterwards to reflect and decide what to build to make the systems easier to manage. The author says SRE plays the role of pilot and engineer/designer at the same time; experience becomes code packaged as a product, reusable by other SRE teams and even outside Google (Google Cloud). The core responsibilities are consistent over time (reliable, flexible, easy to manage in an emergency, well monitored, with planned capacity), but the typical activities evolve: the example is that "building a dashboard for 20 machines" becomes "automating discovery, dashboards and alerts across a fleet of tens of thousands of machines". Analogy: a hundred years ago the airplane had one engine (two, with luck), a pilot who was also mechanic and loader, and the failure of any system was catastrophic (p.324); today a 747 with hundreds of passengers, redundant systems and a 6,000-mile flight still has only two pilots (p.325). [from source] (SRE p.324-325) [DATED] for the 2016 numbers.

Ch. 1 (p.23): Ben Treynor Sloss joined Google in 2003 and managed a "Production Team" of seven engineers; SREs are now seen as software engineers who design operations. For the limit of 2 events per 8-12 h shift and the playbook (~3x MTTR improvement), see the sections above. (SRE p.23, 25-26)

Contrast with "launch and iterate" (p.319). In detailed requirements gathering and design, the former defense contractor described a culture in which creating a new defense system usually meant an entire year of design, followed by only three weeks writing the code; the book says this is very different from Google's "launch and iterate" culture, which promotes a much faster pace of change with calculated risk, and that other industries (medicine, military) have very different pressures, risk appetites and requirements, which inform their processes. It is not "more reliable/recommended": it is fit to context. In the laser surgery machine example, requirements are gathered from surgeons and technicians because the designer neither operates nor maintains the equipment. (SRE p.319)
CAPA (p.319): *corrective and preventative action* corresponds to blameless postmortem culture; see postmortem-e-rastreamento-de-outages.md.

Preparation strategies (p.317-319): organizational focus on safety (at the synthetic diamond factory every management meeting began with safety; very detailed software standards and safety integrity levels SIL 1-4 in nuclear, military aircraft and railway signaling), attention to detail (submarine: a lubricating oil maintenance failure can become a major failure), swing capacity (telecom: "switch on wheels"; unpredictable event such as the 2005 leak of a celebrity's phone that generated DDoS symptoms), simulations and drills (aviation uses simulators with real feeds because it cannot test "in production"; telecom runs hurricane drills; the nuclear Navy runs drills "weekly, two to three days a week", breaking real things with control parameters; lifeguards use a "mystery shopper": staged drowning), training and certification (lifeguards: rigorous certification and recertification, site-specific training), requirements gathering and defense in depth (nuclear: redundancy in all systems and a final physical barrier). DiRT: Google forces real outages to make sure the systems react as thought, find weaknesses and avoid uncontrolled outages. (SRE p.317-319)

Regulation and near misses (p.320): agencies cited: FCC, FAA, OSHA, FDA and competent EU authorities. At Alcoa, the CEO required being notified within 24 hours of any injury that cost a day of work and gave his personal phone number to the workers. *Near misses* are scrutinized as a "preventive postmortem" ("latent error + enabling condition"); the British CHIRP program collects confidential reports in aviation and maritime and publishes analyses in bulletins; lifeguards write a report after any incident (if feet enter the water, there will be paperwork) and, in traumatic cases, call a counselor. Automation and decision (p.320-322): nuclear Navy with a human decision chain (to operate a valve, an operator, a supervisor and a crew member on the phone with the engineering officer); trading more cautious (Knight Capital, Flash Crash); manufacturing in favor of automation for efficiency and repeatability; British nuclear 30-minute rule; LASIK (data sanity check and iris matching eliminated a class of errors). Structured decision: basis agreed in advance, clear inputs, explicit assumptions, data beats the opinion of the most senior (HiPPO); other industries "if it ain't broke, don't fix it", follow "the binder" (checklists for every imaginable scenario, suited to slow industries or those with limited-skill labor), controlled experimentation (research and manufacturing) or separation of roles (trading: an *enforcement* team separate from the traders shuts the system down in the face of abnormalities and only it turns it back on).
