Preface note 4 (p.20), what it actually says: SRE says it is *distinct from the industry term DevOps*, because, although it treats infrastructure as code, it has reliability as its primary focus and is strongly oriented toward removing the need for operations. The note does not assert rivalry; the statement that the principles are consistent (DevOps as a generalization of SRE, SRE as a specific implementation of DevOps) is in the "DevOps or SRE?" box on p.24. For "it is not rivalry" cite p.24; the note on p.20 only supports the difference in focus. (SRE p.20, 24)

Terminology and topology (p.28). A *machine* is a piece of hardware (or a VM); a *server* is software that implements a service; any machine can run any server, and allocation is done by the cluster operating system, Borg. Dozens of machines form a rack; racks sit in rows; one or more rows form a cluster; a datacenter building normally houses several clusters; nearby buildings form a campus. Inside the datacenter, the Clos network called Jupiter connects hundreds of switches and supports up to 1.3 Pbps of bisection bandwidth between servers in the largest configuration; between datacenters, the global backbone B4 is a software-defined network (OpenFlow) with massive bandwidth for a modest number of sites and elastic bandwidth allocation. (SRE p.28)

Hardware failures and Borg (p.29-30). In a cluster, in a typical year, thousands of machines and thousands of disks fail; the software abstracts this from users. Borg is a distributed cluster operating system, similar to Apache Mesos, that runs jobs (permanent servers or batch such as MapReduce) made up of one or thousands of identical tasks; if a task misbehaves, it is killed and restarted, possibly on another machine. Because tasks move, BNS (Borg Naming Service) is used, with paths such as /bns/<cluster>/<user>/<job>/<task> that resolve to IP:port. Borg bin-packs tasks according to the requested resources and considering failure domains (it does not put all of a job's tasks in the same rack, so the rack's top-of-rack switch is not a single point of failure) and kills a task that uses more resources than it requested (a slow crashloop is preferable to a task that was never restarted). (SRE p.29-30)

Storage (p.30). Layers: D (fileserver on almost every machine, disk and flash), Colossus (cluster filesystem with replication and encryption, successor to GFS) and, on top of it, Bigtable (petabyte NoSQL, sparse sorted map indexed by row, column and timestamp, with eventually consistent replication across datacenters), Spanner (SQL-like interface for those who need real consistency worldwide) and others such as Blobstore, each with its trade-offs (see data integrity). (SRE p.30)

Network, GSLB, Chubby and Borgmon (p.32). OpenFlow SDN network with simple switches and a duplicated central controller that precomputes the best paths; Bandwidth Enforcer (BwE) manages bandwidth. GSLB balances at three levels: geographic for DNS requests, at the user service level (YouTube, Maps) and at the RPC level; the service owner provides a symbolic name, the list of BNS addresses and the capacity at each location (in QPS). Chubby is the lock service with a filesystem-like API, uses Paxos, helps elect the master among replicas and stores the BNS mapping. Borgmon collects ("scrapes") metrics for alerts, behavior comparison and capacity planning. (SRE p.32)

Software infrastructure and RPC (p.32-33). The code is heavily multithreaded; every server has an HTTP server with diagnostics and statistics. All services communicate through an RPC infrastructure called Stubby, whose open source version is gRPC (note 11); RPC is often used even for local calls, which makes it easier to refactor to another server. Data travels in protocol buffers, "similar to Apache's Thrift", and the book says that, compared with XML, they are simpler to use, 3 to 10 times smaller, 20 to 100 times faster and less ambiguous (the comparison is with XML, not with JSON). (SRE p.32-33)

Development environment (p.33). Except for some groups with their own open source repositories (Android and Chrome), Google engineers work from a single shared repository [Pot16]. Practical consequences: whoever finds a problem in a component outside their project can fix it, send the *changelist* (CL) to the owner for review and submit it to mainline; changes to the project's own code require review and all software is reviewed before being submitted. Build requests go to build servers in the datacenter, which compile in parallel; the same infrastructure runs continuous tests: for each submitted CL the tests of everything that depends on it, directly or indirectly, run, and the owner is notified if the change probably broke something; some projects use push-on-green. (SRE p.33)

Shakespeare example and life of a request (p.33-35). Batch component (MapReduce in three phases map, shuffle and reduce, writing the index to a Bigtable) plus an always-on frontend; the user resolves the DNS, GSLB chooses the IP of the Google Frontend (GFE, reverse proxy that terminates TCP), the GFE finds the Shakespeare frontend via GSLB and sends the HTTP via RPC, the frontend calls the backend (BNS address via GSLB), which queries Bigtable; the chain takes a few hundred milliseconds, and a faulty GSLB would cause damage. The book attributes reliability to rigorous testing policies, careful rollout and proactive error recovery, such as graceful degradation. (SRE p.33-34)

Sizing (p.35). Load test: a backend handles about 100 QPS; the predicted peak is 3,470 QPS, so at least 35 tasks, and N+2 gives 37; per region, 17 in the US, 16 in Europe, 6 in Asia and 4 (N+1, not 5) in South America, saving 20% of that region's hardware at the cost of a small latency risk (details in the Ch. 2 numbers section). (SRE p.35)

Notes 9 to 13 (p.35). Note 9: datacenter hardware is homogeneous "more or less", since some datacenters accumulate generations of hardware and are expanded after they are ready. Note 11: gRPC is at grpc.io. Note 12: protocol buffers are an extensible, language- and platform-neutral mechanism for serializing structured data (note 40 of Ch. 9, p.84, repeats this definition; see toil-automacao-e-simplicidade.md). Note 13: the probability of two simultaneous task failures is assumed to be low enough to be negligible, but single points of failure, such as top-of-rack switches or power distribution, can invalidate this assumption in other environments. (SRE p.35)

The book notes that stability and agility are often in tension in the SRE world, but here stability drives agility: with the build predictably solid and reliable, developers iterate faster; without it, release cadences such as nightly and weekly builds lose value and responding to an emergency release (e.g. a security vulnerability) becomes more complex and difficult. [from source] (SRE p.139-140)
Barriers against risky software; test DR and repair tools; statistical tests (Lemon, Chaos Monkey, Jepsen) are not repeatable by nature. [from source] (SRE p.140-142)
Simple tests in seconds; the 42,000 tests calculation: to accept 99% of perfect patches, each test must be right more than 99.9999% of the time. [from source] (SRE p.142-143)
Release cadence: an annual release gives an MTBF of one year; testing intermediate versions gives confidence; "reliability budget" per team. [from source] (SRE p.143-144)
Configuration: files changed only on failure vs changed more than once per release; noisy break-glass mechanism. [from source] (SRE p.144)

Config in an interpreted language (interpreted languages, e.g. Python, common because the interpreter can be embedded and there is simple sandboxing against non-malicious errors) is risky: the file's content is, for testing purposes, potentially hostile to the interpreter, and there are latent flaws that are hard to handle once and for all. Loading the config is executing a program, so there is no inherent upper bound on the inefficiency of loading. How to test: pair the integration test with rigorous deadline checking in all integration test methods, marking as failed the tests that do not finish in a reasonable time. [from source] (SRE p.145)

Alternatives: own text syntax requires coverage of all test categories from scratch; YAML with a heavily tested parser (Python's safe_load) removes part of the toil and, with good choice of syntax and parser, gives a hard upper bound on load time; but schema gaps are left to the implementer, and the simple strategies for that have no time limit and rarely have robust unit tests. Protocol buffers: the schema is defined beforehand and checked automatically at load, removing more toil and keeping time bounded. Since any tool can fail from bugs the tests do not catch, the book advises defense in depth (another tool or a tested validator should report the misbehavior; report, not always fix). [from source] (SRE p.145)

Production probes: known bad, known good replayable, known good non-replayable; integrated into the readiness check; combinations of probe and application versions. What it means for the probe to fail: the probe in production runs a configuration that was never tested before (the release test uses a frontend with a fake backend; the probe uses the release binary with a balancer in front and a real persistent backend; frontends and backends have independent release cycles). It should never fail; if it fails, the frontend API (coming from the balancer) or the backend API (to the persistent storage) is not equivalent between production and the release environment and, unless the reason is already known, the site is probably broken. The same production updater that swaps the application swaps the probes gradually, continuously generating the four combinations (old/new probe × old/new application); it detects the combination that generates errors and rolls back to the last known good state. With the probe included in the readiness check, the update fails indefinitely, no user traffic reaches the new version and it stays paused until engineers diagnose it and take the updater to a clean rollback. [from source] (SRE p.145-146)
Fake backend and compatibility between peer versions. [from source] (SRE p.146)
Testing is one of the most profitable investments for reliability. [from source] (SRE p.146)

Blaze is Google's build tool (C++, Java, Python, Go, JavaScript): it defines targets (e.g. a JAR) and their dependencies and builds the dependencies automatically; Rapid passes flags such as the build identifier; every binary accepts a flag that shows build date, revision and identifier. Note 37 (p.81) says Blaze was open-sourced as Bazel. Hermetic = insensitive to libraries installed on the machine; depends on known versions of compilers and dependencies; the build tools themselves are versioned by the project revision, so a cherry pick from last month does not use this month's compiler. (SRE p.77-78, 81)

In Ch. 17 the book returns to Bazel as an example of a tool with more precise control of tests: it creates dependency graphs; when a file changes it rebuilds only what depends on it; builds are reproducible and only the tests of the changed code run, cheaper and faster (p.140; note 93 on p.147). [from source]

The book does NOT carry a Maven to Bazel migration plan, BUILD/WORKSPACE files, pom.xml, commands or rules; only the hermetic/reproducible principle, the internal use of Blaze and these two mentions of Bazel.

Other details of Ch. 8: "Push on Green" (deploy of every build that passes all tests) and hourly builds with version selection by test results (p.77); MPM packages with stage labels (dev, canary, production) that migrate to the new package when the label is reapplied (p.78); Rapid configured by "blueprints" with ACLs by role; serial or parallel workflows; dispatch to Borg tasks (p.78-79); Sisyphus for complex rollouts (a rollout is a logical unit of one or more tasks; it can update everything at once or successive clusters over several hours) (p.79-80); release velocity metrics (time until a change reaches production) (p.76); example of configuration in its own package: flag first_folio replaced by bad_quarto via cherry pick without rebuilding the binary, with label much_ado to install both packages together (p.80).

Rule of thumb of note 89 (p.147): start with 0.1% of traffic and increase by orders of magnitude every 24 h, varying the geographic location (day 2: 1%, day 3: 10%, day 4: 100%). Note 90 says that, with continuous exponential growth from 1% to 10% in 24 h, the time for traffic to grow by a factor of e is about 10 hours and 25 minutes [checked: 24 h ÷ ln 10 ≈ 10.4 h]. Canary model in the body text: the cumulative number of variation reports grows as a power of the failure order U: U=1 simply broken code, U=2 the request corrupts data that a future request will see, U=3 the corrupted data is also a valid identifier of an earlier request; most bugs are of order 1 and grow linearly with traffic (on p.139 the exponents were lost in the PDF; use only the idea; the book writes "172%" for the factor and, without recomputing; the fn90 of p.147 is readable: K = 86,400 ÷ ln(0.1/0.01) = 37,523 s, i.e. 10 h 25 min 23 s, and the book says about 10 h 25 min; 10 h 23 min would be a conversion error). High-order bugs must be caught at release, or the operational load grows too fast. (SRE p.139, 147)

Unit tests cost milliseconds on a laptop; bringing up a full server with dependencies takes minutes to hours; performance test example: a program going from 8 GB to 32 GB of memory or from 10 ms to 50 ms and 100 ms of response without anyone noticing. Configuration tests: one per versioned file, comparing production with the file; they get more complex when there are defaults embedded in the binary, preprocessing (bash for flags) or shared runtime context. (SRE p.137-138)

When the build breaks, everyone should drop everything else and fix it: it is harder to fix later, it slows the team down, it makes nightly/weekly builds lose value and complicates an emergency release (p.140). Barrier defenses for risky software (3 steps: a barrier that makes the replica fail the health check; risky software only accesses unhealthy replicas; a validation tool removes the barrier) (p.141). Automation tools also need testing (e.g. a container balancer that tries to move itself; upgrade and rebalancing tools with a circular dependency) (p.141). Offline DR tools: checkpoint equivalent to a clean stop, loadable, with barrier and clean start (p.141-142).

Statistical tests (Lemon, Chaos Monkey, Jepsen) are not repeatable; recording the random generator seed and redoing the run as a release test helps measure how hard it will be to prove the failure was fixed (p.142). The 42,000 tests calculation: a service with more than 21,000 simple tests compares the result vector before and after the patch (21,000 + 21,000 = 42,000); if rejecting 1 patch in 10 causes outrage and 1 in 100 goes unnoticed, you want to accept 99% of perfect patches: the 42,000th root of 0.99 requires each test to be right more than 99.9999% of the time (p.142-143). [checked: 0.99^(1/42000) ≈ 0.99999976]

An annual release had an MTBF of one year "no matter how much testing"; testing intermediate versions gives a mappable cause and a shorter feedback cycle; the "reliability budget" can be segmented by functionality or team (SRE has a separate one). A config file that only changes on failure has a cadence slower than the MTBF; one that changes more than once per app release dominates reliability if it does not have better coverage than the app; noisy break-glass (open a bug) that does not turn off the tests (associates the push with the pending test and annotates afterwards). (SRE p.143-144)

Example of /etc/passwd read halfway: the tool that maintains home directories must report the discrepancy and not "remediate" by deleting user data (p.145). Probes: the production updater gradually swaps application and probes, generating the four combinations (old/new probe × old/new app); if the probe is part of the readiness check, the update fails forever and no user traffic goes to the new version until the team diagnoses it (p.146). Fake backends maintained by the peer's team and monitoring aware of the versions on both sides of the interface (p.146); only the new combinations (result of a new release of one of the sides) need to run, and this need not block the release itself, but rollout automation should, ideally, block the production rollout until the problematic combinations are no longer possible; the peer team's automation may consider draining (and updating) the replicas that have not yet left the problematic combination (p.146).

Why the release branch with cherry-pick exists (p.78). Code goes to mainline; the branch is cut at a specific revision and is never merged back. Fixes go into mainline first and are cherry-picked to the branch. The stated reason: avoid mistakenly picking up unrelated changes submitted to mainline after the original build; this way "we know the exact contents of each release". Attention: the direction is *mainline → branch*; it is not "avoid dragging changes from the branch into main" (that reading inverts the book). (SRE p.78)

Why rerun the tests on the branch (p.78). The test targets of the continuous build must match those that block the release, and the release must be created at the revision of the last continuous build that passed all tests (less chance of failure in the release build). Even so, at release the unit tests run again on the branch, with an audit trail that all passed: if the release has cherry picks, the branch may contain a version of the code that exists nowhere in mainline, and you want the guarantee that the tests pass in the context of what is actually released. In addition there is an independent test environment that runs system tests on the packaged artifacts, triggered by hand or by Rapid. (SRE p.78)

Packaging in MPM (p.78). Packages assembled from Blaze rules (artifacts, owners, permissions), with a name (e.g. search/shakespeare/frontend), versioned with a unique hash and signed to guarantee authenticity; Rapid applies a label with the build ID, which makes the package uniquely referenceable by name + label; phase labels (dev, canary, production) move automatically to the new package when reapplied.
The book does not say what the hash algorithm is (nor the signer's): questions about it are NOT COVERED for the detail.

Canary: two distinct scenarios in the book. (1) Ch. 17: rule of thumb (note 89, p.147) of starting with 0.1% of traffic and increasing by orders of magnitude every 24 h. (2) Ch. 27 (p.268): almost every Google update is gradual; a new server is installed on a few machines of a datacenter, observed for a defined period, then on all machines of that datacenter, observed again, and finally globally; the first stages of the rollout are called canaries; the tools that manage installations observe the newly started server and roll back automatically if the change does not pass validation. The book therefore does not limit the canary to "traffic, not machines": Ch. 17 talks about a fraction of traffic and Ch. 27 about a few machines; what it does not give is a fixed percentage of machines. For Android apps the equivalent is releasing the version to a subset of installs and raising the percentage to 100%. See the 6 feature flag requirements in lancamentos-e-capacity-planning.md. (SRE p.147, 268)

Notes of Ch. 17 (p.147). Note 86: after the engineer defines tests in a generalized way, the rest of the work is common to all SRE teams and becomes shared infrastructure: a scheduler (divides budgeted resources among unrelated projects) and executors (sandbox the test binaries so they are not treated as trusted). Note 94: an example in which the synchronous API started returning a *future* and argument errors only appear when the future is evaluated, so many incorrect uses slip through. Note 95: the focus is on SRE tools that need to be scalable; the others should also be tested, with a strategy similar to user-facing applications. Note 98: even repeating the test with the same seed, there is no serialization between task deaths and fake traffic, so there is no guarantee of exercising the observed code path again. Note 102: tools that cross technology verticals and layers of abstraction have a weak association with many software teams and a slightly stronger one with systems teams. (SRE p.147)

SRE tools have two characteristics: their side effects stay within the already tested main API and they are isolated from user-facing production by an existing validation and release barrier. Software that bypasses the normally tested API (example: a database engine that allows temporarily turning off transactions to shorten maintenance windows) can cause havoc if released by mistake against a user-facing replica. The defense design has 3 steps: (1) use a separate tool to put a barrier in the replication configuration, so that the replica fails the health check and is not released to users; (2) configure the risky software to check the barrier at startup and only access unhealthy replicas; (3) use the tool that validates the replica's health (the one from black-box monitoring) to remove the barrier. (SRE p.141)

Automation tools (index selection, balancing across datacenters, shuffling relay logs) have "out-of-band" risk and subtler tests: the operation uses a robust, tested API, but the goal is a side effect that is a discontinuity invisible to another API client; documented invariants (such as a DNS cache retaining results until the TTL) may not hold across the operation. Tools that touch each other's environment (the fleet upgrade one and the container rebalancing one) create a circular dependency, acceptable if the APIs have restart semantics, there is test coverage for them and the checkpoint health is independently ensured. Disaster recovery tools can be designed to operate offline: they compute a checkpoint state equivalent to cleanly stopping the service, push it to be loadable by the normal validation tools and use the usual release barriers. (SRE p.141)

Before, software shipped once a year, with binaries produced over hours or days by a chain of compilation and tests done by people against written instructions; the release effort was dominated by documentation, data migration and retraining. The MTBF of those releases was one year, "no matter how much testing there was": so many changes per release that some user-visible defect would be hidden; in practice, the reliability data of the previous release was irrelevant to the next. (SRE p.143)

Today API/ABI management tools and interpreted languages allow building and running a new version every few minutes. In principle an army of testers could validate each incremental version by the same criterion; the annual version ships with higher quality because the intermediate versions are also tested: the team maps the problems found unambiguously to the causes and is confident that the whole problem, and not just the exposed symptom, was fixed; the principle of the short feedback cycle also applies to automated test coverage. (SRE p.143-144)

The central sentence of p.144: if you let users experience more versions of the software during the year, the MTBF suffers (gets worse), because there are more opportunities for user-visible breakage; in return you discover areas that would benefit from more test coverage, and each implemented test protects against a future failure. Careful reliability management combines the bounding of uncertainty by test coverage with the bounding of user-visible failures to tune the cadence; this combination maximizes the knowledge gained from operations and users, which in turn drives test coverage and release velocity. That is, the thesis that "more released versions raise the MTBF" contradicts p.144; the gain lies in smaller, testable batches with a mappable cause. (SRE p.144)
Do not confuse with p.135: there, more "zero MTTR" bugs (caught by a test that blocks the push) raise the MTBF seen by users; it is another mechanism, the block before production. (SRE p.135)

If an SRE changes a configuration file or the strategy of an automation tool, the work follows the same conceptual model as a user feature; when defining cadence by reliability, it is advisable to segment the "reliability budget" by functionality or, more conveniently, by team: the feature team pursues an uncertainty limit tied to its target cadence, and the SRE team has its own budget and uncertainty, hence its own release rate ceiling. (SRE p.144)

To remain reliable without scaling the number of SREs linearly with the service, the production environment needs to run mostly unattended, and for that it needs to be resilient to minor failures. When a serious event requiring manual SRE intervention happens, the tools used have to be well tested; otherwise the intervention reduces confidence that historical data holds for the near future, and this loss of confidence forces waiting for analysis of monitoring data to eliminate the uncertainty. Hence the conclusion of the passage: testing determines how often it is appropriate to use the tool against production. (SRE p.144)

Do not confuse with p.329 (App. B): there the text says that non-emergency rollouts should be supervised (monitored by the stage engineer or, preferably, by monitoring proven to be reliable) and that, faced with unexpected behavior, you revert first and diagnose afterwards. Supervising a rollout (p.329) and letting the environment run unattended day to day (p.144) are complementary ideas. (SRE p.144, 329)

Configuration files exist because changing configuration is faster than rebuilding the tool, which helps keep MTTR low; from a reliability viewpoint, a file that only changes on failure has a release cadence slower than the MTBF (uncertainty about whether each manual edit is optimal), and a file that changes more than once per app release (for example because it holds release state) dominates the site's reliability if it does not have test coverage and monitoring far better than the app's. (SRE p.144)

Context: configuration is an area of close collaboration between release engineers and SREs; it seems a deceptively simple problem, but configuration changes are a potential source of instability, and the approach evolved considerably. All schemes keep the configuration in the main source code repository and impose a strict code review requirement. Project owners choose the model case by case. (SRE p.80)

1. Mainline. It was the first method used to configure services on Borg (and in earlier systems): developers and SREs change the files at the head of the main branch; changes are reviewed and then applied to the running system. Advantage: binary release and configuration change are decoupled, and it is simple in theory and in procedure. Disadvantage: it tends to generate skew (divergence) between the configuration version in the repository and the one running, because jobs need to be updated to pick up the changes. (SRE p.80)

2. Config and binary in the same MPM package. Suitable for projects with few configuration files or whose files (or part of them) change every release cycle. Advantage: it simplifies deploy, since a single package is installed. Disadvantage: it limits flexibility, because it ties binary and configuration together. (SRE p.80)

3. Separate MPM configuration packages. It applies the hermetic principle to configuration: since configurations tend to be tightly tied to binary versions, build and packaging are used to take a snapshot of the configuration along with the binary; the build ID lets you reconstruct the configuration at a point in time. With two packages (binary and configuration) each changes independently: if the feature shipped with the flag first_folio and later it turns out it should be bad_quarto, you cherry pick onto the release branch, rebuild only the configuration package and deploy, without a new binary build. The MPM label, such as much_ado, indicates which versions of the packages are installed together; since the label is unique in the package namespace, only the most recent package with that label is used. (SRE p.80)
4. External store. For projects whose files need to change frequently or dynamically (with the binary running); they live in Chubby, Bigtable or the source-based file system. (SRE p.80)

In summary, the book presents four options and says each project decides which works best; the only declared common denominator is main repository plus strict code review. The book points to the skew of the mainline model as a concrete defect and the loss of flexibility of the single package. (SRE p.80)

The book does not label any of the four models an "anti-pattern" nor say that "configuration without review is an anti-pattern" in general terms: p.80 only says all schemes require strict code review, and the passages on p.76-81 do not use the word anti-pattern.

Rapid has workflows that define the release actions; actions run in series or in parallel and a workflow can launch others; work is dispatched to tasks of a Borg job in production, which allows thousands of simultaneous release requests. Typical steps: (1) create the release branch from the requested integration revision number (often obtained from the continuous testing system); (2) Rapid uses Blaze to compile all binaries and run the unit tests, often in parallel, in dedicated environments separate from the workflow's Borg job; (3) the artifacts become available for system testing and canary, and a typical canary brings up a few jobs in production after the system tests; (4) each step is logged and a report of all changes since the last release is generated. Rapid also manages release branches and cherry picks, which can be approved or rejected case by case. (SRE p.79)

Deploy: Rapid drives simple deploys by updating Borg jobs to the new MPM packages, according to the deploy definitions in blueprint files and specialized task executors; for complicated deploys Sisyphus is used (a rollout automation framework built by SRE, with extensible Python classes, control panel and tracking), and Rapid creates a rollout in a long-running Sisyphus job, passing the MPM package build label. (SRE p.79-80)

Stated objective: fit the deploy process to the service's risk profile: in development or pre-production, hourly builds and automatic push when all tests pass; in large user-facing services, start in one cluster and expand exponentially until all are updated; in sensitive infrastructure, extend the rollout over several days, interleaving instances from different geographic regions. (SRE p.80)

Note 36 is tied to the sentence on p.77 about hermetic builds ("the same product, at the same revision of the source code repository, on different machines, gives identical results"): the text of the note, on p.81, says Google uses a unified monolithic source code repository (monolithic unified source code repository), with a reference to [Pot16]. This is consistent with Ch. 2, where engineers work from a single shared repository, except groups with their own open source repositories, such as Android and Chrome (p.33). (SRE p.77, 81, 33)

P.77 also gives the reason for high release velocity: releasing frequently results in fewer changes between versions, which makes testing and diagnosis easier; some teams do hourly builds and choose the version to deploy by test results and the features present, and others adopt "Push on Green". (SRE p.77)

Automation tools (database index selection, balancing across datacenters, shuffling relay logs for fast remastering) have two characteristics: the operation is done against a robust, predictable and well-tested API, and the purpose of the operation is the side effect, a discontinuity invisible to another API client. Testing shows the desired behavior of the other layer before and after the change, and it is often possible to test whether the internal state seen by the API is constant throughout the operation (for example, databases chase correct answers even without a suitable index). But some documented API invariants may not hold across the operation: a DNS cache that keeps the result until the TTL is the book's example; if a runlevel switch replaces the local nameserver with a caching proxy, both promise to retain complete lookups for many seconds, but it is unlikely that the cache state is passed from one to the other. (SRE p.141)

The book's question: in what environment do these tools run? The automator that shuffles containers to improve utilization tends to shuffle itself if it also runs in a container; it would be embarrassing if a new version of its internal algorithm generated dirty memory pages so fast that the mirroring network bandwidth prevented completing the live migration. Even if there is an integration test in which the binary deliberately displaces itself, the test probably does not use a production-sized model of the container fleet and almost certainly cannot use the scarce high-latency intercontinental bandwidth to test these races. (SRE p.141)

Even more fun: an automation tool may change the environment in which another runs, or the two may change each other's environment at the same time. Example: the fleet upgrade tool consumes the maximum of resources when pushing upgrades, which would tempt the container rebalancer to move it, and the rebalancer in turn needs an upgrade from time to time. This circular dependency is acceptable if the APIs have restart semantics, someone remembered to implement test coverage of that semantics and the checkpoint health is independently guaranteed. (SRE p.141)

Disaster recovery tools can be designed to operate offline with five constraints: offline, checkpoint, loadable, barrier and clean start. If any of them is broken, it becomes much harder to show confidence that the tool will work at any moment, in the short term. Online repair tools operate outside the main API and are therefore more interesting to test: a hard point is knowing whether normal, eventually consistent behavior interacts badly with the repair; the offline tool usually expects instantaneous consistency, which is easier to test, and a unified instrumented binary may be needed to observe the transactions. (SRE p.142)

Maven→Bazel migration plan, BUILD/pom.xml files and Bazel commands (the book only names Blaze/Bazel, p.78, 81 n.37, 140, 147 n.93); test pyramid with proportions; numeric coverage target; contract testing by name; dark launch/shadow traffic in this chapter (dark launch appears in Ch. 32); flaky test quarantine policy.

Past a certain point, more reliability makes the service worse: it limits feature velocity and raises cost; users do not notice the difference because their experience is dominated by less reliable components (e.g., the cellular network). [from source] (SRE p.37)
Cost is not linear: one increment can cost 100x the previous one; two cost dimensions: redundant resources and opportunity cost. [from source] (SRE p.37)
Principle: "reliable enough, but no more reliable than needed"; the goal is a minimum and a maximum at the same time. [from source] (SRE p.37)
The book focuses on unplanned downtime, expressed in nines; each additional nine is an order of magnitude toward 100%. [from source] (SRE p.38)
Time-based availability = uptime / (uptime + downtime). [from source] (SRE p.38)
Aggregate availability (by requests, rolling window, e.g., one day) = successful requests / total requests. [from source] (SRE p.38)
Examples from the text: 99.99% per year allows 52.56 min of downtime; 2.5M requests/day with a daily target of 99.99% allow up to 250 errors. [from source] (SRE p.38)

At Google the time-based metric usually makes no sense (global services, almost always partially "up"); the success rate (yield) is used. Targets are quarterly, tracked weekly or daily. [from source] (SRE p.38)
Error budget = 1 − availability target (99.99% → 0.01% budget). [from source] (SRE p.25; p.330)
Example: SLO of 99.999% of queries per quarter → budget of 0.001%; a problem that fails 0.0002% of queries consumes 20% of the quarter's budget. [from source] (SRE p.43)
Cost example: 99.9% → 99.99% = +0.09%; with $1M of revenue, that is worth $900; it only pays off if the extra nine costs less than that. [from source] (SRE p.40)
Heuristic: use the background error rate of ISPs (measured between 0.01% and 1%) as a noise floor. [from source] (SRE p.40) [DATED]

Consumer: questions (expected level, link to revenue, paid/free, competitors, consumer/enterprise); the type of failure matters (constant low rate vs total outage); cost is a key factor; other metrics (latency) give degrees of freedom. [from source] (SRE p.39-40)

Infrastructure: infrastructure has several customers with different needs; making it ultra-reliable for all of them is usually too expensive. Bigtable example: consumer services that serve data on the user's request want low latency and high reliability; offline analytics teams (MapReduce) want throughput. What each one wants from the request queue: the low-latency user wants the queue (almost) always empty, to process each request on arrival (an inefficient queue is a common cause of tail latency); the offline analytics user wants the queue never empty, so the system is never idle waiting for the next request. One's success is the other's failure. [from source] (SRE p.41)

Solution in the example: partition the infrastructure into independent tiers, two kinds of cluster: low latency (with plenty of capacity slack, less contention, more redundancy and customer isolation) and throughput (run "hot", with less redundancy); the second meets the relaxed needs at a much lower cost, perhaps only 10-50% of the cost of a low-latency cluster (that is, the throughput cluster costs 10% to 50% of the other). Key strategy: offer explicitly delineated service tiers, which externalizes the cost difference to customers and motivates them to choose the cheapest tier that meets their needs; Google+ can put privacy-critical data in a globally consistent datastore (Spanner-like) and optional data in a cheaper NoSQL (Bigtable-like). Several tiers run on identical hardware and software, varying the amount of resources, the degree of redundancy, geographic constraints and, critically, the configuration of the infrastructure software. [from source] (SRE p.41)
Tension between dev (velocity) and SRE (reliability), amplified by information asymmetry; typical tensions: fault tolerance, testing, push frequency, canary duration/size. [from source] (SRE p.42)

Procedure: product defines a per-quarter SLO; actual uptime is measured by a neutral third party (monitoring); the difference is the budget; while budget remains, releases continue. [from source] (SRE p.42-43)
Budget exhausted: releases are temporarily suspended and resources go to testing/resilience; subtler alternatives to on/off exist (slow down, roll back). [from source] (SRE p.43)

Network outages or datacenter failures that reduce the measured SLO also consume the budget; the number of pushes can be reduced for the rest of the quarter and the whole team supports it, since everyone shares responsibility for uptime. [from source] (SRE p.43)
Requires SRE to have the authority to stop launches; the product team becomes self-policing. [from source] (SRE p.43)
If the SLO gets in the way of launching features, it can be loosened. [from source] (SRE p.43)

Appendix B: period "often a month"; once exhausted, freeze changes except urgent security fixes and bugs that address the cause; for an SLO > 99.99% a quarterly reset is appropriate because the allowed downtime is small; the budget is described as a common, data-driven mechanism to assess the risk of launches and gives SRE and development the shared goal of innovating faster without "blowing the budget". [from source] (SRE p.330). Note: Ch. 3 speaks of a quarter, App.
B of "often a month"; the book does not reconcile them.
SLI: a quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service (latency, error rate, throughput). [from source] (SRE p.44)
Availability = fraction of time usable, often the fraction of successful requests (yield); durability = probability that data is retained over the long term. [from source] (SRE p.44)
SLO: a target value or range for an SLI. [from source] (SRE p.45)

Not every SLI becomes an SLO (p.45): the book says the SLO value is not always chosen; for HTTP requests coming from outside, QPS is determined essentially by users' desire, so no SLO is set for QPS; average latency per request, however, can be the object of a target. The book's example of a "fast" SLO uses average search latency below 100 ms (the book itself uses the average in this example; the caveat about averages vs percentiles comes later, p.46-47; 100 ms is declared an arbitrary value). QPS and latency can be linked: more QPS tends to increase latency and there is a "performance cliff" above a certain load. [from source] (SRE p.45) [inference: that is why QPS enters as capacity-planning data and not as an SLO target; see p.175-176 and p.188-192]

SLA: a contract (explicit or implicit) with consequences, most easily recognized when financial (rebate, penalty); test: "what happens if the SLO is not met?" — with no explicit consequence, it is an SLO. [from source] (SRE p.45)

Targets by service type: a typical Google Apps for Work service would have an external quarterly target of 99.9%, backed by a stronger internal target and by a contract with penalties; YouTube in 2006 got a lower target than the enterprise one, being a consumer product still changing and growing fast (SRE p.39). The published target of Google Compute Engine was "three and a half nines": 99.95% (SRE p.44).

Latency: an SLO on a 100 ms average hides the tail; example from Fig. 4-1: the typical request takes ~50 ms, but 5% of requests are 20 times slower; a system that serves 200 req/s on even seconds and 0 on odd seconds has the same average as a constant 100 req/s, but peaks of 200; example SLOs: 99% of Get RPCs in under 100 ms; 90% in under 1 ms and 99% in under 10 ms; 99.9% in under 100 ms; 95% of Set from throughput clients in under 1 s; 99% of Set from latency clients with payload < 1 kB in under 10 ms (SRE p.45-48). Standardized aggregation: "1-minute average", "measured every 10 seconds".

Tail (Ch. 6): with average latency of 100 ms at 1,000 req/s, 1% of requests may take 5 s; if 1% of requests are 50x the average, the rest are about twice as fast as the average (note 23); a backend's p99 can become the frontend's median (SRE p.58, 62). For a 99.9% annual target (which allows ~9 hours of aggregate downtime per year; per the App. A table it is 8.76 h), probing for status 200 more than once or twice per minute is probably unnecessary, and checking disk occupancy more often than every 1-2 minutes also is (two distinct rules; only the disk one is "every 1-2 min"); a 1-min window for CPU hides long spikes that feed the tail (SRE p.59).
Background error rate example: ISPs between 0.01% and 1% (SRE p.40); 99.9% → 99.99% is worth $900 on $1M of revenue (0.09% × $1M) (SRE p.40).

The appendix's recommendation (p.328). Using an aggregate unavailability metric ("X% of all operations failed") is more useful than focusing on outage duration in two cases: services that can be partially available, for example because they have several replicas and only some are unavailable, and services whose load varies over the day or week rather than staying constant. The appendix refers to the time-based and aggregate availability equations of Ch. 3. (SRE p.328)

The two equations (p.38). Time-based availability is the proportion of time the system is up (uptime ÷ (uptime + downtime)), and the App. A table (p.326-327) converts nines into minutes of downtime. But, at Google, a time-based metric usually makes no sense for globally distributed services, because it is very likely that at least part of the traffic is being served somewhere in the world at any moment (the service is at least partially "up"); therefore availability is defined by the request success rate (yield): successful requests ÷ total, over a rolling window. (SRE p.38)

When to use each. App. A opens by saying that availability is generally computed from the time the service was unavailable in a period and that the table (p.326-327) assumes no planned downtime; the closing note (p.328) adds that, for a partially available or variable-load service, the aggregate metric is more useful than duration. (SRE p.326-328)

[inference] The same minutes of outage weigh differently if they fall at peak or in the small hours, which explains the preference for the aggregate metric when load varies; this is the package's reading, not a sentence from the book.

Burn rate, multi-window alerts, "error budget policy" as a document, SLO per critical user journey, comparison of rolling vs calendar window as a design choice (p.38 only mentions a one-day rolling window), a table beyond 5 nines; the "1 − SLO" formula appears only in words. All of this is [extrapolation] (later Workbook/practice).

Definition: work tied to running a production service that tends to be manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly as the service grows. Not every task has all the attributes. [from source] (SRE p.51)

It is not toil: work one dislikes, administrative overhead (team meetings, setting and grading goals, snippets, HR paperwork) and "grungy" work with long-term value (e.g., cleaning up alert configuration). [from source] (SRE p.51)

Manual includes running by hand a script that automates the task: it is faster than executing each step, but the human hands-on time spent running the script (not the elapsed time) is still toil. Repetitive: a task done for the 1st time, or even the 2nd, is not toil. [from source] (SRE p.51)
Overhead (the book's list): hiring, HR paperwork, team/company meetings, bug queue hygiene, snippets, peer reviews and self-assessments, training courses. [from source] (SRE p.53)
Six criteria: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, no enduring value, O(n) with service growth. [from source] (SRE p.51-52)
Goal: toil below 50% of each SRE's time; at least 50% on engineering. [from source] (SRE p.52)

Floor calculation: with 1 week of primary and 1 of secondary per cycle, a 6-person rotation gives a floor of 2/6 = 33% of time; with 8 people, 2/8 = 25% (lower bound of potential toil). [from source] (SRE p.52)
Largest reported sources: interrupts, on-call, releases/pushes. Quarterly survey: average ~33%, with outliers from 0% to 80%. [from source] (SRE p.52) [DATED]
Activity categories: software engineering, systems engineering, toil, overhead. [from source] (SRE p.52-53)

Harms of excess toil: career stagnation, low morale, confusion about the role, slowdown, precedent (devs push operations onto SRE), friction, broken promises to those who joined for projects. In small doses it is not bad. [from source] (SRE p.53)
Beware of "requires human judgment": it can be a design failure (a service that alerts several times a day). [from source] (SRE p.53-54, note 21)

Values: consistency, platform, faster repairs (MTTR), faster action, time savings ("decoupling operator from operation"). [from source] (SRE p.63-64)
Automation is a "force multiplier", not a panacea; better still is a system that does not need automation (autonomous). [from source] (SRE p.63)

Hierarchy of classes (example: DB master failover): (1) none, (2) SRE script maintained outside the system, (3) generic automation maintained outside, (4) internal, specific automation, (5) system that needs no automation. [from source] (SRE p.66)

"Maximalist" view and its limits (p.65) [from source]: Google has an ideological inclination to use machines to manage machines (and controls the whole stack, since the code is almost always available), but the book admits reality demands adjustment: it is not appropriate to automate every component of every system, not everyone has the ability or willingness to develop automation at a given moment, and some essential systems were born as quick prototypes, not designed to last or to interact with automation. The previous paragraph describes a maximalist position, put into practice with broad success in Google's context; the general choice was to build platforms, or to position itself to build platforms over time, seen as necessary for manageability and scale. (SRE p.65)

Rarely executed automation and bit rot (p.66) [from source]: turnup automation is usually kept separate from the core system and suffers bit rot (it does not change when the system changes); trying to couple the two more tightly fails because of misaligned priorities, since developers rightly resist requiring a test deployment on every change; in addition, automation that is crucial but runs only occasionally, and is therefore hard to test, is especially fragile because of the long feedback cycle. Classic example of rare automation: cluster failover, which may happen only every few months, or so rarely that inconsistencies between instances accumulate. (SRE p.66)
High abstractions are easy to manage but "leak": case of a binary push that assumes atomicity. [from source] (SRE p.65)

Ads/MySQL on Borg case: manual failover of 30-90 min per instance was incompatible with the error budget (at best 99% uptime; the budget called for <30 s per failover); the "Decider" daemon (2009) did failover in <30 s in 95% of cases; cost: all applications gained much more failure-handling logic (custom JDBC); mundane operational work dropped ~95%, with automated schema changes the total maintenance cost fell nearly 95%, and ~60% of the hardware was freed. Details in the section "Automation cases with numbers and narrative". [from source] (SRE p.66-67)
Prodtest and idempotent fixes: each test paired with an idempotent fix that can run every 15 minutes; lessons on latency between test and fix producing flaky tests. [from source] (SRE p.68-70)

Competence / latency / relevance triangle: automation kept away from those who operate loses relevance and competence; bad incentives arise when the owning team is not accountable for the automation. [from source] (SRE p.70-71)
Admin Servers / Local Admin Daemon: authenticated RPC with ACLs, code review and auditing instead of root SSH. [from source] (SRE p.72) [DATED]

Evolution of turnup automation in 5 stages (p.72, the book's own list) [from source]: 1. manual action triggered by an operator (no automation); 2. system-specific automation, written by the operator; 3. generic automation maintained externally; 4. system-specific automation, maintained internally; 5. autonomous systems that need no human intervention. Do not confuse with the failover list on p.66. (SRE p.72)

Bigtable initial disk case (implicit safety signal): automation wiped disks of Bigtable machines because it assumed "unused disk = machine with no storage"; replicas prevented loss. [from source] (SRE p.68). Bit rot of turnup automation maintained outside the system: (SRE p.66)
Diskerase case: the empty set was interpreted as "all machines"; lessons: sanity checks, rate limiting, idempotent workflow. [from source] (SRE p.74; also Ch. 13, p.119-120)
Recommendation: automating does not require Google scale; the biggest lever is in design; autonomy is hard to retrofit. [from source] (SRE p.74)

Counter-risk: when automation fails, the operator has lost fluency and a mental model (reference to Air France 447); train with drills (Air France 447 and drills are in notes 33 and 35, printed on p.75). [from source] (SRE p.73-75)
Perfect stability only in a vacuum; SRE balances agility and stability; exploratory code with an expiry date may sacrifice stability. [from source] (SRE p.82)
"The virtue of boring": surprises in production are the nemesis of SRE; essential vs accidental complexity (Brooks); SRE should resist the accidental. [from source] (SRE p.82-83)

Commented-out code and dead code guarded by a permanently disabled flag are bad ideas (the book cites Knight Capital and the SEC order; the loss figure, US$ 440 million in a few hours, is in Ch. 33, p.321-322); every line is a liability; removal routine and bloat detection in tests. [from source] (SRE p.83)
"Negative lines of code" metric; minimal APIs; modularity and API versioning; avoid "util"/"misc" binaries. [from source] (SRE p.83-84)
Simple releases: small batches make it easier to attribute cause (analogy with gradient descent). [from source] (SRE p.84)

Modularity (p.84): release cadence can vary between parts of the system, without requiring a full push for every change; the separation of responsibilities between APIs and binaries matters more as the system grows, in direct analogy with object-oriented design: just as a "grab bag" class with unrelated functions is bad practice, so is putting a "util" or "misc" binary into production; a well-designed distributed system has collaborators with a clear, bounded purpose. Modularity also applies to data formats: one of the central strengths of Google's protocol buffers was creating a wire format that is backward and forward compatible. Note 40 (p.84): protocol buffers ("protobufs") are an extensible, language- and platform-neutral mechanism for serializing structured data; the text is the same as note 12 of Ch. 2 (p.35), but note 40 is the one that accompanies Ch. 9. [from source] (SRE p.84)
Saying "no" to a feature keeps the environment free for real engineering. [from source] (SRE p.84)
Ads MySQL on Borg and the Decider (SRE p.66-67).

Context: the Ads database ran on MySQL; from 2005 to 2008 it was in a "mature and managed" state (the replica swap routine was already automated). In late 2008 the team built a proof of concept of MySQL on Borg, hoping to (1) eliminate machine/replica maintenance, since Borg restarts tasks, and (2) pack several instances onto the same physical machine with containers. (SRE p.66-67)

The problem: tasks move on Borg once or twice a week; tolerable for replicas, unacceptable for masters. Master failover took 30 to 90 minutes per instance; with shared machines, reboots for kernel upgrades and normal failures, there would be several unrelated failovers per week. That, added to the number of shards, meant: manual failover would consume many human hours and give, at best, 99% availability, below the business requirement; and, to fit in the error budget, each failover would have to cause less than 30 seconds of unavailability, and "there was no way to optimize a human-dependent procedure to under 30 seconds". The book's conclusion: the only way out was to automate failover. (SRE p.67)

The solution: in 2009 Ads SRE finished the failover daemon "Decider", which performed planned and unplanned failovers in under 30 seconds 95% of the time. The team went from optimizing the infrastructure for the absence of failover to accepting that failure is inevitable and optimizing for fast recovery through automation. (SRE p.67)

Admitted cost: all applications needed much more failure-handling logic than before; since the MySQL world assumes the instance is the most stable component, software such as JDBC had to be customized to tolerate a failure-prone environment. (SRE p.67)

Benefits: time spent on mundane operational tasks fell 95%; a database task going down stopped paging a human; later, with schema change automation, the total operational maintenance cost of Ads Database fell nearly 95%; migrating to MoB (MySQL on Borg) freed resources by scheduling several instances per machine: about 60% of the hardware freed. "We automated ourselves out of a job." (SRE p.67)
Cluster turnup, Prodtest and idempotent fixes (SRE p.67-72).

Cluster turnup: steps from preparing the building to assigning resources to services; some services had more than a hundred subsystems and complex dependencies; configuring one subsystem differently from the others is "a customer-impacting outage waiting to happen". A multi-petabyte Bigtable cluster was configured to not use the first (log) disk on 12-disk machines; a year later an automation assumed "first disk unused = machine with no storage" and instantly erased all the Bigtable data (the real-time replicas were saved): automation must not rely on implicit safety signals. (SRE p.68)

Prodtest extended the Python unit-testing framework to test real services, with chained tests (one failure aborts the following ones), per cluster; it generates a graph of the states; each delay caused by another team's misconfiguration becomes a bug to extend Prodtest. For the first time managers could predict when a cluster would go "live" and understand why each cluster took six weeks or more from "network-ready" to serving traffic. Senior management's mission: within three months, five new clusters would be network-ready on the same day and should be turned up in one week ("One Week Turnup"). (SRE p.68-70)

Each test was paired with an idempotent fix, which could run every 15 minutes without risk; if a fix fails several times the automation stops and notifies; it made it possible to go from "network works and machines in the database" to "serving 1% of search and ads traffic" in one to two weeks. In retrospect there were flaws: the latency between test, fix and new test created flaky tests, and not every fix was naturally idempotent. (SRE p.70)

The competence / latency / relevance triangle: it started with a competent process (maintained by the owners), high latency and very relevant; when centralized in a turnup team, there were more than a thousand changes per day in the affected systems, the automation lost relevance and competence, and bad incentives arose (whoever speeds up turnup is not accountable for the service's technical debt). The way out: a security mandate replaced SSH with Admin Servers (authenticated local daemon, with ACLs, RPC and code review; each change is auditable) and then turnup became a service-oriented architecture problem: each owner exposes a turnup/turndown API (contract); the process became competent, accurate and low-latency even as the number of teams and services doubled every year. (SRE p.70-72) [DATED]

Borg and the "warehouse-scale computer": thousands of machines are born, die and go to repair daily without SRE effort; rescheduling a task onto another machine looks like a process switching CPUs, an intrinsic feature of the system and not something to "automate". If automation takes the place of manual actions and they continue to be presumed, operators lose fluency and mental model (note 33: Air France 447; note 35: drills). (SRE p.72-74)

Diskerase (SRE p.74; also p.119-120): the decommissioning of a rack failed after Diskerase; on restarting from the beginning, the set of machines to wipe was (correctly) empty, but the empty set was a special value meaning "everything": almost all machines in all colos were sent to Diskerase; within minutes the CDN lost its disks and stopped terminating connections; users were served by the company's own datacenters and only a small latency increase was seen, thanks to good capacity planning; most of two days to reinstall the machines in the affected colo and weeks to audit and add sanity checks, including rate limiting, and to make the decommissioning workflow idempotent. (SRE p.74)

Value of automation (Ch. 7): consistency ("the value of consistency is in many ways the primary value"), platform (a bug fixed once), faster repairs (lower MTTR; a defect found later costs more), faster action and time savings ("decoupling the operator from the operation"); for Google, services would not survive without automation, as they crossed the threshold of manual operation long ago. (SRE p.63-64)

Ch. 9 (p.83): the proposals "comment out the code", "guard it with a flag" instead of deleting are "terrible"; version control reverts changes easily, and code that never executes, guarded by an always-off flag, is "a time bomb", as Knight Capital experienced; the reference is the SEC order "In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC" ([Sec13]).

Ch. 33 (p.321): automation can cause a lot of damage and financial loss in very little time; "in 2012 Knight Capital Group experienced a 'software glitch' that led to a loss of US$ 440 million in a few hours"; note 160 (printed on p.322) points to section "FACTS", B, of the SEC order, about the Power Peg software. In the same paragraph: the 2010 Flash Crash (attributed to a trader trying to manipulate the market by automated means) caused a loss "on the order of trillions of dollars in 30 minutes" in the market, which recovered quickly (note 161). The book's lesson: "speed can be negative if the tasks are poorly configured". (SRE p.321-322)
Any "45 minutes" does not come from the book [extrapolation].

Note 21 (p.53): beware of "it is not toil because it requires human judgment": one must check whether the nature of the task really requires judgment and cannot be solved by better design; the example is a service that alerts SREs several times a day, each alert requiring a complex response with a lot of judgment: it is a poorly designed service. (SRE p.53)

Notes of Ch. 7 (p.74): note 27 says that the expertise gained when building an automation has value of its own (the engineers understand the automated process deeply and automate new processes faster afterward); note 30 recalls that not every managed system exposes callable APIs, which forces certain tools to use a CLI or "automated clicks on websites"; note 26 warns that those who already know the value of automation can go straight to "The Value for Google SRE", but that the description has useful nuances. (SRE p.74)

Automation is "meta-software" (software that acts on software); examples of use: user account creation, cluster turnup and turndown, preparation and decommissioning of installations, version rollouts, runtime configuration changes (including of dependencies). In SRE the focus is usually the lifecycle of systems (for example, deploying a service to a new cluster), and not the quality of the data passing through the infrastructure, although gross differences are alerted on (half of a dataset disappearing after a push). Tools such as Puppet, Chef, cfengine and even Perl differ mainly in level of abstraction; the trade-off is classic: high abstractions are easy to manage, but when they "leak" the failure is systemic and can be inconsistent (a supposedly atomic binary push can leave binaries prepared but not shipped, shipped but not restarted, or restarted but not verifiable). The book acknowledges that it is not appropriate to automate everything and that some essential systems were born as prototypes; the preference is to build platforms. (SRE p.65)

Figure 7-1 (p.69): ProdTest of the DNS service. Shows how a failing test aborts the chain of following tests: Prodtest tests have dependencies on each other, forming a chain, and the failure of one quickly stops those that depend on it. The text introducing it is on p.68. Figure 7-2 (p.71) shows the DNS ProdTest in which a failed test resulted in running only one fix. (SRE p.68-71)

How Prodtest is used (p.68). Each team's Prodtest receives the cluster name and validates that team's services in that cluster. Later it became possible to generate a graph of the unit tests and their states: the engineer quickly sees whether the service is well configured in all clusters and, if not, why; the graph highlights the step that failed and the failing Python test emits a more detailed error message. (SRE p.68)

Delay caused by another team: bug to extend Prodtest (p.68). Whenever a team suffered a delay from another team's unexpected misconfiguration, a bug was opened to extend that team's Prodtest, so that a similar problem would be discovered earlier in the future; this is prevention, not the blocking mechanics of the fix. (SRE p.68)

From test to fix (p.70). The unit test already knew which cluster it was examining and which test was failing, so each test was paired with a fix. If each fix were idempotent and could assume its dependencies were satisfied, solving the problem would be easy and safe; requiring idempotent fixes meant teams could run the "fix script" every 15 minutes without fear of damaging the cluster configuration. (SRE p.70)

The DNS example with the Machine Database (p.70). If the DNS team's test was blocked by the configuration of a new cluster done by the Machine Database team, as soon as the cluster appeared in the database the DNS tests and fixes began to work. It is a dependency block that resolves itself when the other team finishes; it is not a test that "aborts everything". (SRE p.70)

The names in the DNS example (Figure 7-2, p.70). In the DNS example, if TestDnsMonitoringConfigExists fails, FixDnsMonitoringCreateConfig is called, which scrapes the configuration from a database and checks a skeleton configuration file into the revision control system; then TestDnsMonitoringConfigExists passes on retry and TestDnsMonitoringConfigPushed can be tried; if this fails, FixDnsMonitoringPushConfig runs. If a fix fails several times, the automation assumes the fix failed, stops and notifies the user. (SRE p.70)

Result and flaw (p.70). With these scripts a small group of engineers went from "the network works and the machines are listed in the database" to "serving 1% of search and ads traffic" in one or two weeks, which seemed the pinnacle of automation technology; looking back, the approach had a fundamental flaw: the latency between test, fix and second test created flaky tests that sometimes passed and sometimes failed, and not every fix was naturally idempotent, so an unstable test followed by a fix could leave the system in an inconsistent state. (SRE p.70)

Before Prodtest (p.68). The creative, fragile shell scripts did not answer readiness questions: were the service's dependencies available and correctly configured? Were all configurations and packages consistent with other deployments? Could the team confirm that every configuration exception was desired? An example of an effect: a flag that made GFS more responsive to log processing leaked into the default templates and cells with many files could run out of memory under load. (SRE p.68)

Why the example matters for teaching (p.68-70). Project managers began to predict when a cluster would go live and to understand why each cluster took six weeks or more from "network-ready" to serving traffic; that visibility, plus the mission "five clusters network-ready on the same day, turned up in one week", motivated the idempotent fixes. (SRE p.68-70)

The duration in minutes of the Knight Capital incident (the book gives only "a few hours" and US$ 440 million); a formal toil budget; GitOps/Kubernetes as an automation practice (infrastructure as code appears only in note 4 of the preface, p.20; Kubernetes in note 10, p.35); complexity metrics; a quantitative rule for when to automate.
